blocks.html: Chemistry is the study of matter: anything that has mass and takes up space. Air, water, your desk and your own body are all matter. The first question a chemist asks about any sample is simple: is it one substance, or several mixed together? The answer depends on the particles (atoms and molecules) too small to see.

A pure substance has a fixed makeup. An element has only one kind of atom; a compound has two or more elements bonded in a fixed ratio. A mixture holds two or more substances whose amounts can vary: homogeneous if it looks the same throughout (salt water), heterogeneous if you can see separate parts (sand in water).

In a compound, atoms are bonded into identical units. Every water molecule is two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom, so every sample of pure water, from any place, is 11.2% hydrogen by mass. In a mixture, nothing is bonded together; the particles are only mingled, so you can add a pinch more salt or a little more water and still call it salt water. That is also why physical methods (filtering, boiling, using a magnet) can separate a mixture but cannot split a compound.

blocks.title: Two clear liquids
blocks.q: Distilled water and salt water both look clear and the same all the way through. Classify each.

Water has one kind of molecule, $\mathrm{H_2O}$, in which the atoms are bonded. It has its own properties: it is a liquid at room temperature, while the gas mixture is not.
blocks.a: No. The gases are a mixture; water is a compound made when they react.

blocks.html: Water can be ice, liquid or steam, yet the molecules are the same $\mathrm{H_2O}$ in all three. Elements, Compounds and Mixtures sorted matter by what it is made of; here we sort it by how its particles are arranged and how they move. The particle model says that matter is made of tiny particles that are always moving and that attract each other.

In a solid, particles are packed close and vibrate about fixed positions. In a liquid, they are still close but slide past each other. In a gas, they are far apart and fly freely in straight lines between collisions. Heating makes the particles move faster; it does not make them bigger.

Two things compete: the attractions between particles, which pull them together, and their motion, which pulls them apart. When motion is weak compared with the attractions, the particles are held in place (solid). With more energy they can roll past each other but stay touching (liquid). With enough energy they break free completely (gas). That is why a solid keeps its shape, a liquid keeps its volume but flows, and a gas fills any container and can be squeezed: most of a gas is empty space.

blocks.html: In Solids, Liquids and Gases you saw that melting and boiling change how particles are arranged but not what they are. Some changes go deeper: the atoms come apart and join up in new ways. That is the line between a physical change and a chemical change.

A physical change alters form, size or state, but the substance stays the same (ice melting, sugar dissolving, a can being crushed). A chemical change (a chemical reaction) makes new substances with new properties (wood burning, iron rusting, an egg cooking). At the particle level, a chemical change regroups the atoms; no atoms are created or lost.

What a substance is depends on how its atoms are bonded. Boiling water only pulls $\mathrm{H_2O}$ molecules apart from each other, so the vapor is still water and condenses back into water. Burning methane breaks the bonds in $\mathrm{CH_4}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$ and forms new ones, giving $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O}$: different molecules with different properties. You cannot get the methane back by cooling.

blocks.html: These are clues, not proof: a color change can also come from mixing dyes, and bubbles also appear in boiling water. The real test is whether a new substance formed.

blocks.title: Bubbles two ways
blocks.q: Water bubbles when it boils. Baking soda bubbles when vinegar is poured on it. Which is a chemical change?
steps: The bubbles in boiling water are water vapor, the same substance as the liquid: physical.
The bubbles from baking soda and vinegar are carbon dioxide, a gas that was not there before: chemical.
blocks.a: Only the baking soda and vinegar.

blocks.title: Dissolving salt
blocks.q: Is dissolving salt in water a chemical change? The salt disappears.
steps: The salt’s ions spread out among the water molecules, but they are still the same ions.
Boil the water away and the salt is left behind, unchanged.
blocks.a: No: dissolving is a physical change.

blocks.html: Calling boiling or dissolving chemical because bubbles appear or something seems to vanish, or treating every color change as a reaction. Ask one question each time: is there a new substance at the end, made by regrouping atoms? If you could get the original back by a physical step (cooling, evaporating), it was a physical change.

blocks.html: Scientists around the world use one system of units, the SI (from the French Système International). Its base units include the meter (m), kilogram (kg), second (s), kelvin (K) and mole (mol). To describe very large or small amounts, SI adds a prefix, and each prefix is just a power of ten, the same powers you used in Multiplying and Dividing by Powers of 10 and Scientific Notation.
A prefix stands for a power of ten: replace it with that power. $2.5\ \text{km} = 2.5 \times 10^{3}\ \text{m} = 2500\ \text{m}$. Converting to a smaller unit gives a bigger number.

blocks.html: A prefix is a multiplier glued to a unit. "k" means "times 1000", so a kilometer is 1000 meters, just as a dozen eggs is 12 eggs. When you measure the same length with smaller units, you need more of them: 1 km is 1000 m, and 1 m is 100 cm. So a number grows when its unit shrinks, and the amount itself never changes.

blocks.html: Every measurement has some uncertainty. A ruler marked every millimeter cannot tell you a length to the nearest thousandth of a millimeter. Scientists show how exact a measurement is by how many digits they write. You already know Rounding Decimals; significant figures tell you where to round.

Record all the digits you are sure of plus one estimated digit. Those are the significant figures. Nonzero digits always count; zeros between them count; leading zeros never count; trailing zeros count when there is a decimal point.

Digits carry information about the measurement. In $0.0045\ \text{m}$, the zeros only place the decimal point: the same length is $4.5\ \text{mm}$, with no zeros at all, so they cannot be significant. In $2.50\ \text{g}$, the final 0 says the balance read the hundredths place and found 0 there, which is real information: writing $2.5\ \text{g}$ would claim less.

blocks.html: Once you know how to record a measurement (Measurements and Significant Figures), the next question is how good it is. Two different words describe that, and they mean different things.

Accuracy: how close a measurement is to the true (accepted) value. Precision: how close repeated measurements are to each other. Percent error measures accuracy: $$\%\ \text{error} = \dfrac{|\text{measured} - \text{accepted}|}{\text{accepted}} \times 100\%.$$

Think of darts. If all your darts land in a tight bunch, you are precise, even if the bunch is far from the bullseye. If they average out around the bullseye but are scattered, you are accurate on average but not precise. A balance that was never zeroed reads every mass a little high: precise (the readings agree) but not accurate. Percent error divides by the accepted value because that is the fixed reference everyone compares with, as in Percent Error.

A consistent offset like this points to a balance that needs zeroing (a systematic error).

Repeating a measurement shows precision only; you need the accepted value to judge accuracy. Check the percent-error formula: the denominator is the value you trust, not the one you are testing.
Some books keep the sign of the error (negative when the measurement is low). Here we report its size.

blocks.html: A calculator will happily give you ten digits, but an answer can be no more certain than the measurements that went into it. You know how to count Measurements and Significant Figures and how to compute with scientific notation; now combine them.

Multiplying or dividing: keep as many significant figures as the measurement with the fewest significant figures. Adding or subtracting: keep as many decimal places as the measurement with the fewest decimal places. Round once, at the end. Counted and defined numbers are exact and never limit the answer.

When you add, the uncertain digits line up by place value: $12.52 + 3.1$ is uncertain in the tenths place, because 3.1 tells you nothing about hundredths. So the sum is known only to the tenths: $15.6$. When you multiply, uncertainties scale with the size of the numbers, so what matters is the relative uncertainty, which is set by how many significant figures each factor has. Rounding at every step stacks small rounding errors, so keep extra digits until the end.

blocks.html: In Units and Conversion Factors you multiplied by conversion factors. Chemists use that one idea for almost every calculation in this course, from grams to moles to liters of gas, so it is worth making automatic. It works with SI Units and Metric Prefixes and with any other units.

A conversion factor is a fraction equal to 1, such as $\dfrac{1000\ \text{m}}{1\ \text{km}}$. Multiply by factors arranged so the units you don't want cancel (one on top, one on the bottom), leaving the units you want.

Since $1000\ \text{m}$ and $1\ \text{km}$ are the same length, their ratio is exactly 1, and multiplying by 1 never changes an amount. Units then behave like algebra: $\text{km} \times \dfrac{\text{m}}{\text{km}} = \text{m}$. If the units cancel to what you want, the setup is right; if they don't, you've flipped a factor. For squared or cubed units, the factor is squared or cubed too: $1\ \text{m} = 100\ \text{cm}$, so $1\ \text{m}^3 = 100^3\ \text{cm}^3 = 1{,}000{,}000\ \text{cm}^3$.

blocks.html: Why does a steel ship float while a steel bolt sinks? Why does oil float on water? The answer is density, a Unit Rates that compares how much matter is packed into a space.

Density is mass per unit volume: $d = \dfrac{m}{V}$, usually in $\text{g/cm}^3$ for solids and $\text{g/mL}$ for liquids ($1\ \text{mL} = 1\ \text{cm}^3$). Density is a property of the substance, not of the object, so it can identify what something is made of.

Each substance packs its particles a certain way, and each particle has a certain mass. Take more of the substance and you take more particles and more space in the same proportion, so the ratio of mass to volume stays the same. Cut a gold bar in half: each half has half the mass and half the volume, and the same density, $19.3\ \text{g/cm}^3$. An object floats on a liquid when its average density is less than the liquid's: a ship's hull encloses lots of air, so its average density is less than water's.

blocks.q: Ethanol has a density of $0.789\ \text{g/mL}$. What is the mass of $250\ \text{mL}$?

blocks.title: Water displacement
blocks.q: A stone with mass $40.5\ \text{g}$ raises the water in a cylinder from $25.0\ \text{mL}$ to $40.0\ \text{mL}$. Find its density.
steps: The stone pushes aside its own volume of water: $$V = 40.0 - 25.0 = 15.0\ \text{mL} = 15.0\ \text{cm}^3.$$

blocks.html: Temperature measures how fast the particles of a substance are moving on average: their average kinetic energy. On the Celsius scale, water freezes at $0\ ^\circ\text{C}$ and boils at $100\ ^\circ\text{C}$ (at 1 atm). But 0 °C is not "no motion", so chemists also use a scale that starts at the true bottom. Adding the shift is the same kind of step as adding signed numbers.

The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature, where particle motion is at its minimum. A kelvin is the same size as a Celsius degree: $T_K = T_C + 273.15$. Absolute zero is $0\ \text{K} = -273.15\ ^\circ\text{C}$. Write kelvins without a degree sign: 298 K.

Gas experiments show that as a gas cools, its pressure (at fixed volume) drops in a straight line, and every gas's line points to the same temperature, $-273.15\ ^\circ\text{C}$, where the pressure would reach zero. That is absolute zero. Measuring from there makes temperature proportional to the average kinetic energy of the particles, so ratios mean something: 600 K really is twice as "hot" as 300 K in that sense, while $20\ ^\circ\text{C}$ is not twice $10\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

In kelvins that change is 283 K to 293 K, only about 3.5% more. Whenever a problem compares or multiplies temperatures, convert to kelvins first.
In the United States, everyday temperatures use Fahrenheit: $T_F = \tfrac{9}{5}T_C + 32$, so water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F. Science problems in this course use Celsius and kelvins only.

blocks.html: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures described elements and compounds by their atoms. But how do we know atoms exist, and what is inside one? Nobody can see an atom with ordinary light. Our picture was built in steps, and each step came from an experiment that the older picture could not explain.

Dalton (1808): matter is made of atoms that combine in whole-number ratios. Thomson (1897): atoms contain tiny negative electrons. Rutherford (1911): almost all of an atom's mass and all its positive charge sit in a tiny nucleus; the rest is mostly empty space. Bohr (1913): electrons have only certain energies. Chadwick (1932): the nucleus also holds neutral neutrons.

blocks.name: ch-atom
blocks.cap: The gold-foil experiment: almost every alpha particle passes straight through, and a very few bounce back. Compare with what Thomson’s model predicts.

blocks.html: In Rutherford's lab, Geiger and Marsden fired fast, heavy, positive alpha particles at very thin gold foil. In Thomson's model the positive charge was spread thinly through each atom, so nothing could turn an alpha particle around; every particle should pass through with only tiny deflections. Most did. But a very few, roughly one in several thousand, bounced back. Rutherford later compared it to firing a heavy shell at tissue paper and seeing it come back. Only a tiny, very dense, positive center could do that. Because so few particles hit it, the nucleus must be tiny: about 10,000 to 100,000 times narrower than the atom.

blocks.title: Reading the evidence
blocks.q: What two results of the gold-foil experiment led to the nuclear model, and what did each show?
steps: Most alpha particles passed straight through: most of the atom is empty space.
A few bounced back sharply: the positive charge and nearly all the mass are packed into a tiny region, the nucleus.
blocks.a: Mostly empty space, plus a tiny dense positive nucleus.

blocks.title: A sense of scale
blocks.q: An atom is about 100,000 times wider than its nucleus. If the nucleus were a marble 1 cm across, how wide would the atom be?
blocks.a: About 1 km across, with the electrons spread through that space.

blocks.html: Picturing an atom as a solid little ball, the way Dalton did. Rutherford's results rule that out: an atom is mostly empty space around a tiny, dense nucleus. The "edge" of an atom is set by its electrons, which is why atoms can still bump into each other and take up room.
The modern picture (from the 1920s) keeps Rutherford's nucleus and Bohr's energy levels but treats each electron as a cloud of probability rather than a tiny planet in orbit.

blocks.html: The number of protons, the atomic number $Z$, decides which element an atom is. Every carbon atom has 6 protons; every atom with 6 protons is carbon. A neutral atom has as many electrons as protons, so its charges cancel.

Chemistry happens through electrons, but the electrons are arranged by the pull of the nucleus, and that pull comes from the protons. Change the number of neutrons and the nucleus gets heavier, but its charge, and so the electrons and the chemistry, stay nearly the same. Change the number of electrons and you get an ion of the same element, which can gain its electrons back. Only a change in the number of protons makes a different element, and that takes a nuclear reaction, not a chemical one.

blocks.html: Protons, Neutrons and Electrons showed that protons decide the element. Neutrons are free to vary: atoms of the same element can carry different numbers of them. These versions are called isotopes.

Isotopes have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons. The mass number $A$ counts both: $A = \text{protons} + \text{neutrons}$, so $\text{neutrons} = A - Z$. We write an isotope as $^{A}_{Z}\mathrm{X}$ or as "name-A", like carbon-14.

The mass number counts every particle in the nucleus, and the atomic number counts only the protons, so the difference is the neutrons. Isotopes of one element have the same number of protons, hence the same number of electrons when neutral, and so nearly the same chemistry. That is why carbon-14 in a living thing behaves almost exactly like carbon-12, which is what makes radiocarbon dating work. What differs is the mass, and for some isotopes, the stability of the nucleus.

blocks.html: In Protons, Neutrons and Electrons a neutral atom had equal numbers of protons and electrons. In chemical reactions, atoms often gain or lose electrons. The protons never change in a reaction, so the balance tips and the atom becomes an ion.

An ion is an atom (or group of atoms) with a net charge: $\text{charge} = \text{protons} - \text{electrons}$. Losing electrons makes a positive ion (a cation, such as $\mathrm{Na^+}$). Gaining electrons makes a negative ion (an anion, such as $\mathrm{Cl^-}$). The charge is written as a superscript: number first, then sign.

Electrons are the negative particles, so every electron lost leaves one unbalanced proton (+1), and every electron gained adds −1. The nucleus is deep inside the atom and held together by enormous forces; ordinary chemical energies are far too small to move a proton. That is why only electrons are traded in chemistry, and a sodium ion is still sodium.

steps: It lost 2 electrons: the magnesium ion $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$.

blocks.html: Thinking a positive ion gained protons, or that losing electrons makes an atom negative. Electrons are negative, so losing them leaves the atom more positive. Check with the formula: charge = protons − electrons. Fewer electrons than protons gives a positive number.

blocks.html: The periodic table gives chlorine's atomic mass as 35.45 u, yet no chlorine atom has that mass: chlorine is a mix of Isotopes and Mass Number, about three-quarters chlorine-35 and one-quarter chlorine-37. The table's value is a weighted average, the kind of calculation you did with Finding a Percent of a Number.

$$\text{average atomic mass} = \sum (\text{mass of isotope}) \times (\text{fraction of atoms that are that isotope}).$$ Change each percent abundance to a decimal first. The average lands closest to the most common isotope.

Any real sample has billions of billions of atoms, in the same isotope mix almost everywhere on Earth. If 75.76% of the atoms have a mass of 34.969 u and 24.24% have 36.966 u, then the total mass of 100 atoms is $75.76 \times 34.969 + 24.24 \times 36.966$, and dividing by 100 gives the mass per atom on average. That average is what you need when you weigh out a sample, so it is the number the periodic table lists.

blocks.html: Rutherford's nucleus left a question: how are the electrons arranged around it? Bohr's answer (How We Learned What Atoms Are) was energy levels, or shells. Electrons in higher shells have more energy and are, on average, farther from the nucleus.

Electrons fill the lowest-energy shells first. For the first 20 elements, the shells fill 2, then 8, then 8, then 2. Potassium (19 electrons) is 2, 8, 8, 1, and calcium is 2, 8, 8, 2. The electrons in the outermost shell, the valence electrons, decide how the atom bonds.

Each shell has a limited number of places, and the inner shells, closest to the nucleus, are lowest in energy, so they fill first. The first shell holds 2. The second holds 8. The third shell can eventually hold 18, but after its first 8 electrons the next lowest energy level belongs to the fourth shell, so the 19th and 20th electrons go there. (You will see why in Sublevels and Orbitals.)

blocks.html: Giving potassium the arrangement 2, 8, 9, or picturing electrons circling the nucleus on fixed tracks like planets. After 2, 8, 8 a new shell starts. And a shell is an energy level, not a path: an electron in it has a definite energy but no definite orbit.

blocks.html: Neon signs glow red-orange; sodium streetlights glow yellow; fireworks get red from strontium and green from barium. Each element gives off its own colors. Higher Frequency, More Energy showed that light comes in packets (photons) whose energy grows with frequency. Put that together with Energy Levels and Shells and the colors make sense.

An electron can only have certain energies in an atom. When it drops from a higher level to a lower one, it gives off one photon whose energy equals the gap: $E_{photon} = E_{high} - E_{low}$. Bigger drop, more energetic photon, shorter wavelength (toward violet). Each element's set of gaps gives its own pattern of bright lines.

Energy is conserved: the energy the electron loses must go somewhere, and it leaves as light. Because the levels are fixed, only certain drops are possible, so only certain photon energies come out, and a prism spreads them into separate lines rather than a rainbow. Different elements have different numbers of protons and electrons, so their levels and gaps differ, like fingerprints. Running the process backward, an atom absorbs only photons that exactly match a gap, which is how astronomers read the elements in a star's light.

steps: Level 4 is higher than level 3, so the drop 4 → 2 is bigger and its photon has more energy.
More energy means a shorter wavelength, so 3 → 2 has the longer wavelength.
Indeed 3 → 2 is the red line (656 nm) and 4 → 2 is blue-green (486 nm).

blocks.html: Thinking an atom can give off light of any energy, or that a bigger drop gives a longer wavelength. A bigger drop gives a more energetic photon, and energy and wavelength go opposite ways: violet light has short waves and high-energy photons, red light long waves and low-energy photons.

blocks.html: The shells of Energy Levels and Shells are only the first part of the story. Inside each shell are sublevels of slightly different energies, and inside each sublevel are orbitals. This finer structure explains the 2, 8, 8 pattern and the shape of the periodic table.

Level $n$ has $n$ sublevels: s, p, d, f. An s sublevel has 1 orbital, p has 3, d has 5, f has 7. Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons (with opposite spins). So s holds 2, p 6, d 10, f 14, and level $n$ holds $2n^2$ in all.

Quantum mechanics shows that an electron bound to a nucleus can only take certain wave patterns. The number of patterns grows with the level: level 1 allows one (1s), level 2 allows four (one 2s and three 2p), level 3 allows nine. Each pattern (orbital) can be shared by two electrons only if their spins are opposite (the Pauli exclusion principle). Counting: level 2 holds $4 \times 2 = 8$, level 3 holds $9 \times 2 = 18$. The 3d sublevel is higher in energy than 4s, which is why the third shell stops at 8 for a while.

blocks.cap: Orbital boxes drawn at their energies. Step electrons in for oxygen: each box (orbital) takes at most two arrows, pointing opposite ways.

steps: Level 2 has only 2 sublevels: s and p.

blocks.html: Picturing an orbital as a path the electron travels, or thinking every level holds exactly 8 electrons. An orbital is a region where the electron is likely to be found, a cloud, not a track. And only level 2 holds 8; level 3 holds 18 and level 4 holds 32.

blocks.html: An electron configuration lists how many electrons sit in each sublevel, like $\mathrm{1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^4}$ for oxygen: 2 electrons in 1s, 2 in 2s and 4 in 2p. It uses the sublevels from Sublevels and Orbitals and fills them in order of energy.

Fill sublevels from lowest energy up: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, … The periodic table shows this order: read it row by row, left to right, and each block tells you the sublevel (s block on the left, d block in the middle, p block on the right). The superscripts must add up to the number of electrons.

Electrons take the lowest energies available, just as water fills the bottom of a glass first. The order isn't simply by level number because sublevels overlap in energy: 4s is a little lower than 3d for potassium and calcium, so 4s fills first. The periodic table was built from the behavior of the elements, and its shape matches the filling order exactly: rows of 2, 8, 8, 18, 18 come from s (2), s + p (8) and s + d + p (18).

blocks.html: In 1869 Dmitri Mendeleev arranged the 63 elements then known into a table where similar elements fell into the same column. He left gaps and predicted elements to fill them; gallium (1875) and germanium (1886) were later found with almost exactly the properties he had predicted. Electron Configurations now explains why his table works.

The modern periodic table is ordered by atomic number (number of protons). Columns are groups, numbered 1 to 18; rows are periods. Elements in a group have the same number of outer electrons and behave alike. Each period starts a new outer shell, so the period number is the outermost shell an atom uses.

Chemical behavior comes from the outer electrons. Lithium, sodium and potassium each have one electron beyond a full noble-gas arrangement ($\mathrm{[He]\,2s^1}$, $\mathrm{[Ne]\,3s^1}$, $\mathrm{[Ar]\,4s^1}$), so they react in the same way, and they line up in group 1. Mendeleev ordered by mass, which mostly agrees with the order of atomic number; in 1913 Henry Moseley measured atomic numbers directly and fixed the few places where mass order fails, such as argon (39.95) before potassium (39.10).

blocks.html: Metals (shiny, conduct electricity) fill the left and middle; nonmetals sit at the upper right; the metalloids (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te) lie along the staircase between them.

blocks.q: Give the group and period of bromine.
steps: Bromine is in the column with F, Cl and I: group 17, the halogens.
It is in the fourth row: period 4. Its outer electrons are in shell 4.

blocks.title: Out of mass order
blocks.q: Tellurium (127.60 u) comes before iodine (126.90 u). Why?
steps: The table is ordered by atomic number: tellurium has 52 protons, iodine 53.
Ordering by number of protons also puts iodine with the other halogens, where its chemistry belongs.
blocks.a: Order is by atomic number, not mass.

blocks.html: Thinking the table is ordered by atomic mass, or mixing up groups (columns) with periods (rows). Check: the atomic number goes up by exactly one from each element to the next, while the mass sometimes goes down. A column is like a family that shares behavior; a row is a series of different behaviors.

blocks.html: When atoms react, only their outermost electrons take part; the inner ones are held too tightly. Groups, Periods and Families groups atoms by those outer electrons, so the table tells you how many each main-group atom has.

Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost shell. For main-group elements: groups 1 and 2 have 1 and 2; groups 13 to 18 have the group number minus 10 (3 to 8). Helium has 2. A Lewis dot symbol shows them as dots around the element's symbol, one per side before pairing.

Look at the configurations. Sulfur is $\mathrm{[Ne]\,3s^2\,3p^4}$: its outer shell, shell 3, holds $2 + 4 = 6$ electrons. Selenium, below it, is $\mathrm{[Ar]\,4s^2\,3d^{10}\,4p^4}$: the 3d electrons are tucked inside, in a lower shell, so its outer shell also holds 6. The 10 columns of the d block are the "minus 10". For transition metals the d electrons take part too, so the simple rule does not apply to them.

blocks.html: Atoms are not all the same size. Cesium atoms are more than four times as wide as fluorine atoms. Two things decide the size: how many shells the electrons use, and how strongly the nucleus pulls on them. Both come from Groups, Periods and Families.

Atoms get larger down a group, because each period adds a shell farther out. Atoms get smaller across a period (left to right), because each step adds a proton that pulls the same outer shell in more tightly. So the largest atoms are at the lower left and the smallest at the upper right.

Opposite charges attract more strongly when the charges are bigger and when they are closer (Coulomb's law). Across a period, the outer electrons stay in the same shell while the nuclear charge grows by one each step. The inner electrons shield the outer ones from the nucleus, but the added electrons go into the same outer shell, where they shield each other very little. So the pull on the outer shell grows, and the atom shrinks. Down a group, the new shell is much farther out and more inner electrons shield it, which outweighs the extra protons.

blocks.cap: Sodium and chlorine, both in period 3. Chlorine has 17 protons pulling on its third shell, sodium only 11, so chlorine is smaller.

blocks.name: ch-periodic
blocks.cap: Covalent radius across the table: big at the lower left, small at the upper right.

blocks.title: Across a period
blocks.q: Which is larger, a magnesium atom or a sulfur atom?
steps: Both are in period 3: their outer electrons are in shell 3.
Sulfur has 16 protons, magnesium 12. The bigger nuclear charge pulls sulfur's shell in closer.
Magnesium is larger (measured radii: Mg 141 pm, S 105 pm).

blocks.title: Down a group
blocks.q: Rank lithium, sodium and potassium from smallest to largest.
steps: All are in group 1. Each one down adds a shell: Li uses shell 2, Na shell 3, K shell 4.
Smallest to largest: Li < Na < K.

blocks.html: Expecting atoms to grow across a period because they have more electrons. More electrons does not mean more room: the new electrons go into the same shell, while the extra protons pull that whole shell inward. Check with the periodic table: across a row the shell number stays the same, and the nuclear charge goes up.

blocks.html: To make a positive ion, something must pull an electron off an atom, and that costs energy. How much depends on how tightly the electron is held, which follows the same charge-and-distance reasoning as Atomic Radius.

The first ionization energy is the energy needed to remove the outermost electron from a gaseous atom. It rises across a period (more protons pull on the same shell) and falls down a group (the outer electron is farther away and better shielded). Noble gases have the highest values in their periods; alkali metals the lowest.

The attraction between the nucleus and an outer electron grows with the charge the electron feels and shrinks with distance, like Attraction and Repulsion. Fluorine's outer electrons feel 9 protons from a short distance, behind only two shielding 1s electrons: removing one costs 1681 kJ/mol. Lithium's single outer electron is in the same shell but feels only 3 protons: 520 kJ/mol. Cesium's outer electron sits in shell 6, behind 54 inner electrons: only 376 kJ/mol. No "wanting" is needed to explain any of this.

blocks.name: ch-periodic
blocks.cap: First ionization energy against atomic number. Peaks at the noble gases, drops at each alkali metal; the small dips at B, O, Al and S are real and are explained in General Chemistry.

blocks.title: Across a period
blocks.q: Which has the higher first ionization energy, sodium or chlorine?
steps: Both have their outer electrons in shell 3.
Chlorine has 17 protons pulling on that shell, sodium 11.
Chlorine holds its outer electrons more tightly: 1251 kJ/mol against 496 kJ/mol.

blocks.title: Down a group
blocks.q: Why is the first ionization energy of potassium (419 kJ/mol) lower than that of sodium (496 kJ/mol)?
steps: Potassium's outer electron is in shell 4; sodium's is in shell 3.
It is farther from the nucleus and shielded by 18 inner electrons instead of 10, so it is held less tightly.
blocks.a: It is farther out and more shielded.

blocks.html: Explaining the trend by saying atoms "want" a full shell. An atom has no wants; an electron is held by the pull of the nucleus, and that pull depends on the charge the electron feels and on its distance. Every explanation in this topic should mention charge, distance or shielding.

blocks.html: When two atoms share electrons in a bond, they do not always share evenly. One atom may pull the shared pair toward itself. That pull is electronegativity, and it follows the same pattern as Ionization Energy.

Electronegativity measures how strongly an atom attracts the electrons in a bond. It rises up and to the right on the periodic table. Fluorine is the most electronegative element (3.98 on the Pauling scale); cesium and francium are among the least. Most noble gases are left out because they rarely form bonds.

A bonding pair sits in the outer shells of both atoms. An atom with a large nuclear charge acting at a short distance (upper right) pulls that pair hard, exactly the conditions that make its ionization energy high. Linus Pauling built the scale from measured bond energies: bonds between atoms that differ a lot are extra strong, and the differences give each element a number. The values have no units; only differences between atoms matter.

blocks.html: Ions and Charge showed what an ion is; Valence Electrons and Dot Symbols showed how many outer electrons each atom has. Put them together and you can predict the charge most main-group atoms take.

Main-group atoms gain or lose electrons to reach the electron arrangement of the nearest noble gas. Metals on the left lose electrons: group 1 forms $+1$ ions, group 2 forms $+2$, aluminum $+3$. Nonmetals on the right gain them: group 15 forms $-3$, group 16 $-2$, group 17 $-1$.

It is about energy, not wanting. Removing sodium's one outer electron costs 496 kJ/mol, but removing a second one, from the full inner shell much closer to the nucleus, costs 4562 kJ/mol, far more than any energy the reaction can repay. So sodium stops at $\mathrm{Na^+}$, with neon's arrangement. A chlorine atom releases energy when it gains one electron into its nearly full shell, but a second electron would have to start a new shell farther out, which costs energy. So chlorine stops at $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, with argon's arrangement.

blocks.html: Sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water; chlorine is a poisonous green gas. Together they make table salt. Predicting Ion Charges predicted that sodium loses one electron and chlorine gains one. What holds the resulting ions together?

In an ionic bond, a metal transfers electrons to a nonmetal, and the oppositely charged ions attract. The ions pack into a 3-D lattice in which every positive ion is surrounded by negative ions and every negative ion by positive ones. The formula, NaCl, gives only the ratio of ions (a formula unit); there are no separate NaCl molecules.

Making the ions alone costs energy: removing sodium's electron takes 496 kJ/mol and chlorine gives back only 349 kJ/mol when it gains one. The payoff comes from the lattice. Each $\mathrm{Na^+}$ sits next to six $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ions (and each $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ next to six $\mathrm{Na^+}$), and all those attractions together release about 790 kJ/mol. The solid is far lower in energy than separate atoms, so the compound forms.

steps: One Ca atom loses 2 electrons to become $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$.
Each of the two Cl atoms gains 1. Electrons lost = electrons gained = 2.

blocks.html: Picturing table salt as separate NaCl molecules, each Na stuck to one Cl. In the solid, no sodium ion "belongs" to one chloride ion: each is attracted equally by all six neighbors. The formula only says there is one Na⁺ for each Cl⁻.

blocks.html: An ionic compound has no overall charge. Once you know the charges of its ions from Predicting Ion Charges, the formula follows from making the charges add up to zero. Finding the smallest numbers that do this uses the least common multiple from Greatest Common Factor and Least Common Multiple.

Choose the smallest whole numbers of each ion that make the total charge zero, and write them as subscripts (a 1 is not written). The cation comes first. Aluminum oxide: $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ and $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ balance at a total of 6, so $2 \times (+3) + 3 \times (-2) = 0$ gives $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$.

Any real crystal has to be neutral, or it would be pulled apart by its own charge. So the ratio of ions is fixed by the charges, not by any bonding pattern. A shortcut is to "cross" the charge numbers to become the other ion's subscripts, then reduce: $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ cross to $\mathrm{Ca_2O_2}$, which reduces to CaO.

blocks.name: ch-crystal
blocks.cap: A lattice holds the ions in the ratio that cancels their charges: 1 : 1 when the charges are equal in size.

blocks.q: Write the formula of the compound of $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$.
steps: One $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ carries +2, so it needs two $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ (−2 in total).

blocks.title: Calcium nitride
blocks.q: Write the formula of the compound of calcium and nitrogen.
steps: The smallest total both can reach is 6: three $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ (+6) and two $\mathrm{N^{3-}}$ (−6).

blocks.title: Working backward
blocks.q: What is the charge on iron in $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$?
steps: Two iron ions must carry +6, so each is +3.

blocks.html: Crossing the charges the wrong way, as in $\mathrm{Mg_2Cl}$ for magnesium chloride, or leaving $\mathrm{Ca_2O_2}$ unreduced instead of writing CaO. Check every formula by multiplying back: (number of cations × cation charge) + (number of anions × anion charge) must equal zero, using the smallest possible numbers.

blocks.html: Chemists everywhere name compounds by the same rules (set by IUPAC), so a name tells you the formula. For the ionic compounds of Formulas of Ionic Compounds, the rules are short.

Name the metal cation first, then the nonmetal anion with its ending changed to -ide: NaCl is sodium chloride, $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ is aluminum oxide. Ionic names use no prefixes. For metals that form more than one ion (iron, copper, tin, lead, cobalt and others), add the charge as a Roman numeral: $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$ is iron(III) chloride.

An ionic formula is fixed by the charges, so naming the two ions is enough: once you know "aluminum oxide" means $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ and $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$, only $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ is possible, and prefixes would add nothing. The one gap is a metal with two common charges: "iron chloride" could be $\mathrm{FeCl_2}$ or $\mathrm{FeCl_3}$, so the name must say which iron ion it has.

blocks.q: Name $\mathrm{K_2S}$.
steps: Potassium forms only $\mathrm{K^+}$: no Roman numeral.

blocks.title: A Roman numeral
blocks.q: Name $\mathrm{CuO}$.
steps: Copper forms $\mathrm{Cu^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$, so find the charge.
One $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ carries −2, so the one copper ion is +2.

blocks.html: Using prefixes for ionic compounds (calcium dichloride for $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$), or leaving out the Roman numeral for iron and copper. Remember that the numeral is the charge of the metal ion, not a count of anything: in copper(II) oxide there is only one oxide ion.

Some ions are groups of atoms bonded together that carry one charge as a unit, like the nitrate ion, $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$. They behave like single ions in ionic compounds: the group stays whole, and you balance charges just as before.

A polyatomic ion keeps its own name and formula. To write a compound, balance the charges; if you need more than one of a polyatomic ion, put it in parentheses with the count outside: calcium nitrate is $\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2}$. Never change the subscripts inside the ion.

blocks.html: Inside a polyatomic ion the atoms are held by covalent bonds, and the whole group has a set number of electrons, so its charge is fixed. Changing $\mathrm{NO_3}$ to $\mathrm{NO_6}$ would describe a different (and impossible) particle. Parentheses tell the reader that the subscript outside multiplies the whole group: $\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2}$ has 1 Ca, 2 N and 6 O.

blocks.html: When two nonmetal atoms meet, neither gives up electrons easily: both have high ionization energies (Ionization Energy). Instead they share. You counted the electrons available for sharing in Valence Electrons and Dot Symbols.

A covalent bond is a pair of electrons shared between two atoms. A single bond shares one pair, a double bond two pairs, a triple bond three. More shared pairs make a shorter, stronger bond. Common atoms usually form a set number of bonds: H 1, O 2, N 3, C 4, halogens 1.

A shared pair sits between two nuclei and is attracted to both at once. That attraction pulls the atoms together until the nuclei get so close that they repel each other. The balance point, where the energy is lowest, is the bond length; for $\mathrm{H_2}$ it is 74 pm, and pulling the atoms apart from there takes 436 kJ/mol. The "octet rule" (many atoms end up with 8 electrons around them) is a pattern that results from this, not a reason: atoms don't want anything; bonded atoms are simply lower in energy.

blocks.q: How many bonds does each atom form in water, $\mathrm{H_2O}$?
steps: Oxygen has 6 valence electrons and shares 2 more to be surrounded by 8: two bonds.
Each hydrogen shares its 1 electron: one bond each.

steps: Each N has 5 valence electrons and needs 3 more to be surrounded by 8.
They share three pairs: a triple bond, N≡N.

blocks.html: Saying atoms bond because they "want" eight electrons. The real reason is attraction: shared electrons are pulled by two nuclei, which lowers the energy. That idea also explains things the octet rule can't, such as why bonds have a definite length and why energy is released when they form.

blocks.html: Ionic names don't need counts, because the charges fix the formula (Naming Ionic Compounds). Molecular compounds of two nonmetals are different: nitrogen and oxygen form NO, $\mathrm{NO_2}$, $\mathrm{N_2O}$, $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ and more. With Covalent Bonds there are no charges to balance, so the name itself must count the atoms.

Name the first element, then the second with the ending -ide, and put a prefix on each to give the number of atoms. Leave off mono- on the first element. $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ is dinitrogen tetroxide; $\mathrm{CO}$ is carbon monoxide; $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is carbon dioxide.

The prefixes come from Greek number words, and they are needed because the same pair of nonmetals can combine in several ratios, each a different substance with different properties: carbon monoxide is a toxic gas, carbon dioxide is what you breathe out. Before "oxide", the a or o at the end of a prefix is usually dropped to make the name easier to say: monoxide, pentoxide.

blocks.title: From formula to name
blocks.q: Name $\mathrm{PCl_5}$.
steps: One phosphorus: no prefix on the first element.

blocks.title: From name to formula
blocks.q: Write the formula of dinitrogen pentoxide.
steps: di- means 2 nitrogen atoms; pent(a)- means 5 oxygen atoms.

blocks.title: Ionic or molecular?
blocks.q: Should $\mathrm{SO_3}$ and $\mathrm{Na_2O}$ be named with prefixes?
steps: $\mathrm{SO_3}$: sulfur and oxygen are both nonmetals, so it is molecular: sulfur trioxide.
$\mathrm{Na_2O}$: sodium is a metal, so it is ionic: sodium oxide, with no prefixes.

blocks.html: Using prefixes for ionic compounds, or adding mono- to the first element, as in "monocarbon dioxide". First decide the type: metal + nonmetal is ionic (no prefixes); two nonmetals is molecular (prefixes, but never mono- in front). A few molecules keep common names: water ($\mathrm{H_2O}$), ammonia ($\mathrm{NH_3}$), methane ($\mathrm{CH_4}$).

A Lewis structure is a map of a molecule's valence electrons: lines for shared pairs (bonds) and dots for unshared pairs (lone pairs). It builds on dot symbols from Valence Electrons and Dot Symbols and the bonding from Covalent Bonds, and it is the first step toward predicting a molecule's shape.

1. Count all the valence electrons (add one for each negative charge, subtract one for each positive charge). 2. Connect the atoms with single bonds; the central atom is usually the least electronegative one, never H. 3. Give the outer atoms full octets (H gets 2) with lone pairs. 4. Put leftover electrons on the central atom. 5. If the central atom still has fewer than 8, turn lone pairs from outer atoms into double or triple bonds.

The electron count is fixed by the atoms and the charge: a structure that shows more or fewer electrons than that is describing a different particle. Each step then spends that budget so that every atom ends up surrounded by a full shell, the arrangement that is lowest in energy for these atoms. Moving a lone pair into a shared position (step 5) lets two atoms count the same electrons.

blocks.cap: Carbon dioxide. The electron budget shows 16 valence electrons, all placed; carbon gets its octet from two double bonds.

blocks.title: Water
blocks.q: Draw the Lewis structure of $\mathrm{H_2O}$.
steps: O in the center, bonded to each H: 2 bonds use 4 electrons.
The 4 left go on O as 2 lone pairs. O has 8, each H has 2.
blocks.a: H–O–H with two lone pairs on O.

blocks.title: Carbon dioxide
blocks.q: Draw the Lewis structure of $\mathrm{CO_2}$.
steps: O–C–O uses 4; give each O three lone pairs (12). All 16 are placed, but C has only 4 electrons around it.
Move one lone pair from each O into a bond: O=C=O. Now every atom has 8.
blocks.a: O=C=O, two lone pairs on each O.

blocks.title: An ion
blocks.q: How many valence electrons does the ammonium ion, $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$, have?
steps: The + charge means one electron is missing: $9 - 1 = 8$.

blocks.html: Counting the wrong total, especially for ions (forgetting to add electrons for a negative charge or remove them for a positive one), or giving carbon five bonds. Check every structure twice: count the electrons drawn (2 per line, 1 per dot) against your total, and count the electrons around each atom (no more than 8 for C, N, O and F).

blocks.html: Lewis structures (Lewis Structures) are flat drawings, but molecules are 3-D, and their shapes matter: shape decides whether a molecule is polar, how it packs, even how it smells. The VSEPR model predicts shape from the Lewis structure.

Count the electron groups around the central atom: each bonded atom is one group (a single, double or triple bond counts once), and each lone pair is one group. The groups spread as far apart as possible: 2 groups in a line (180°), 3 in a flat triangle (120°), 4 toward the corners of a tetrahedron (109.5°). The shape is named from the positions of the atoms only.

VSEPR stands for valence-shell electron-pair repulsion. Groups of electrons are all negative, so they push each other as far apart as the central atom allows. A double bond's electrons all sit between the same two atoms, so they occupy one region, one group. Lone pairs are held by one nucleus only and spread out more, so they squeeze the bonds a little closer: water's angle is about 104.5°, not 109.5°.

blocks.cap: Water in 3-D. Drag to turn it: four electron groups point toward the corners of a tetrahedron, but only two hold atoms, so the molecule is bent.

blocks.title: Ammonia
blocks.q: What is the shape of $\mathrm{NH_3}$?
steps: Lewis structure: N with three bonds to H and one lone pair.
4 electron groups, arranged like a tetrahedron.
Only 3 of them are atoms: a pyramid with N at the top.

blocks.title: Formaldehyde
blocks.q: How many electron groups surround carbon in $\mathrm{CH_2O}$ (one C=O double bond and two C–H bonds), and what is its shape?
steps: Three bonded atoms, no lone pairs: 3 groups (the double bond counts once).
3 groups make a flat triangle: trigonal planar, about 120°.

blocks.html: Ignoring lone pairs and calling water linear, or counting a double bond as two groups. Lone pairs take up space even though they don't show in the shape's name. Draw the Lewis structure first, count groups around the central atom, then name the shape from the atoms.

blocks.html: Electronegativity measures how hard an atom pulls on shared electrons. When the two atoms in a covalent bond pull unequally, the shared pair spends more time near one of them.

The electronegativity difference $\Delta EN$ tells how unevenly a bond is shared. A common guide: below 0.4, nonpolar covalent; 0.4 to 1.8, polar covalent; above 1.8, mostly ionic. In a polar bond the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge ($\delta^-$) and the other a partial positive charge ($\delta^+$).

Ionic and covalent bonds are two ends of one range. In $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ the two atoms are identical, so the pair is shared evenly. In H–Cl, chlorine (3.16) pulls harder than hydrogen (2.20), so electron density shifts toward Cl, leaving it slightly negative and H slightly positive. In NaCl the difference (2.23) is so large that the electron has practically moved over: ions. The cutoffs 0.4 and 1.8 are only signposts on that smooth range.

blocks.name: ch-vsepr
blocks.cap: A bond between two atoms. Slide the electronegativity difference from 0 upward and watch the electron cloud shift toward one end.

blocks.title: Classifying
blocks.q: Classify the O–H bond (O 3.44, H 2.20).
steps: Oxygen is more electronegative: O is $\delta^-$, H is $\delta^+$.

blocks.title: Ranking
blocks.q: Rank C–H, C–O and C–F from least to most polar (C 2.55, H 2.20, O 3.44, F 3.98).

blocks.html: Treating ionic and covalent bonds as two separate boxes with a sharp cutoff. A bond with $\Delta EN = 1.7$ is not completely covalent while one with 1.9 is completely ionic; both are strongly polar. Use the guide to name a bond, but think of polarity as a smooth scale.

A molecule can contain polar bonds (Polar and Nonpolar Bonds) and still be nonpolar overall. Whether it is depends on its shape, from Molecular Shapes (VSEPR). Molecular polarity matters because it decides how molecules attract each other, which sets boiling points and what dissolves in what.

Treat each bond dipole as an arrow pointing toward the more electronegative atom. Add the arrows. If they cancel, the molecule is nonpolar; if they leave a net arrow, it is polar. Symmetric shapes with identical outer atoms (linear $\mathrm{CO_2}$, trigonal planar $\mathrm{BF_3}$, tetrahedral $\mathrm{CCl_4}$) are nonpolar.

Bond dipoles add like forces in a tug-of-war. In $\mathrm{CO_2}$ the two C=O dipoles are equal and point in exactly opposite directions, so they cancel. In $\mathrm{H_2O}$ the molecule is bent, so the two O–H dipoles both point partly toward oxygen and add up: oxygen's side of the molecule is negative and the hydrogens' side positive. Change one outer atom and the symmetry breaks: $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ is nonpolar, but $\mathrm{CH_3Cl}$ is polar.

blocks.html: Salt, sugar, diamond and copper are all solids, yet they behave very differently: salt shatters, sugar melts in a pan, diamond scratches glass, copper bends and carries current. The difference lies in what particles the solid is made of and what holds them together, from Ionic Bonds, Covalent Bonds and Solids, Liquids and Gases.

Ionic solids (ions in a lattice): high melting points, hard but brittle, conduct only when melted or dissolved. Molecular solids (separate molecules): low melting points, soft, don't conduct. Network covalent solids (atoms bonded in one giant network): very high melting points, very hard, don't conduct (graphite is an exception). Metallic solids (cations in a sea of electrons): conduct as solids, shiny, can be hammered or bent; melting points vary widely.

To melt a solid you must loosen whatever holds its particles in place. In a molecular solid like sugar or ice, the molecules themselves stay intact; only the weak forces between them must be overcome, so melting is easy. In salt, every ion is held by strong attractions to its neighbors; in diamond, melting would mean breaking covalent bonds throughout the crystal. Electric current needs charged particles that can move: free electrons in a metal, or ions once salt is melted or dissolved. In solid salt the ions are locked in place.

blocks.q: A white solid melts at $801\ ^\circ\text{C}$, shatters when struck, and conducts electricity when dissolved in water but not as a solid. What kind of solid is it?

blocks.q: Why does sugar melt at about $186\ ^\circ\text{C}$ while quartz melts at about $1700\ ^\circ\text{C}$?

Quartz is a network solid: melting requires breaking Si–O covalent bonds throughout the crystal.
blocks.a: Weak forces between molecules against strong covalent bonds.

blocks.html: Thinking a high melting point always means an ionic compound, or that solid salt conducts electricity. Network solids such as diamond and quartz melt even higher than most ionic compounds, and salt conducts only when its ions are free to move, melted or dissolved. Use conductivity as your first clue, then the melting point.

blocks.html: Covalent bonds hold the atoms inside a molecule together. Separate forces act between molecules; they are why water is a liquid and why molecular solids hold together at all. Their strength depends on Polar and Nonpolar Molecules and on size.

London dispersion forces act between all molecules: brief, uneven spreads of electrons attract neighbors, and they grow with the number of electrons. Dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules: the $\delta^+$ end of one attracts the $\delta^-$ end of another. Hydrogen bonds are especially strong dipole attractions between an H bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on an N, O or F of another molecule.

All three are attractions between opposite charges, just smaller and more spread out than in ions. In any molecule the electron cloud jiggles, so for an instant one side is a little negative; that induces the opposite in a neighbor, and the two attract (dispersion). A big molecule with many loosely held electrons does this more strongly. A polar molecule has a permanent $\delta^+$ and $\delta^-$, so it attracts its neighbors all the time. In O–H, N–H and F–H, the H is left almost bare, a tiny, strongly positive point that can get very close to a lone pair: a hydrogen bond. Even so, these forces are much weaker than covalent bonds.

blocks.title: Which forces?
blocks.q: Which forces act between molecules of methanol, $\mathrm{CH_3OH}$?
steps: It is polar (the O–H and C–O bonds don't cancel): dipole–dipole forces.
It has an H bonded to O: hydrogen bonds too.

blocks.title: A near miss
blocks.q: Can fluoromethane, $\mathrm{CH_3F}$, hydrogen-bond to itself?
steps: It contains F, but every H is bonded to C, not to F.
A C–H hydrogen is not positive enough. So no hydrogen bonds: only dipole–dipole and dispersion forces.

blocks.cap: Boiling pulls whole water molecules away from each other. The O–H bonds inside each molecule stay intact.

blocks.html: Thinking that boiling water breaks the O–H bonds inside each molecule. Steam is still $\mathrm{H_2O}$. Compare the energies: boiling a mole of water takes about 41 kJ, while breaking the O–H bonds in a mole of water would take over 900 kJ (about 460 kJ per bond). Boiling only overcomes the forces between molecules.
To boil, a molecule must escape the attractions of its neighbors. So the forces from Intermolecular Forces let you predict which liquids boil higher and which evaporate faster.

Stronger forces between molecules mean a higher boiling point and a lower vapor pressure. To compare: if the molecules are similar in size, the one with stronger kinds of force wins (hydrogen bonding > dipole–dipole > dispersion only). If the kinds are the same, the larger molecule (more electrons) wins. A big enough nonpolar molecule can beat a small polar one.

At a given temperature, molecules have a range of energies, and only those with enough energy to break free of their neighbors escape into the vapor. Strong attractions mean few escape, so the vapor pressure is low and you must heat the liquid further before its vapor pressure reaches the air pressure, which is what boiling is. Size matters because dispersion forces add up over every electron in the molecule: octane ($\mathrm{C_8H_{18}}$, 66 electrons) is nonpolar yet boils at $126\ ^\circ\text{C}$, above water.

blocks.q: Which boils higher, $\mathrm{H_2O}$ or $\mathrm{H_2S}$?
steps: Both are small, bent, polar molecules.

blocks.q: Which has the higher vapor pressure at room temperature, pentane ($\mathrm{C_5H_{12}}$) or octane ($\mathrm{C_8H_{18}}$)?

Pentane is smaller (42 electrons against 66), so its forces are weaker.

blocks.html: Atoms are far too small to count one by one, so chemists count them by weighing, the way a bank counts coins by weighing a bag. The counting unit is the mole. It connects the atomic masses from Average Atomic Mass to grams you can measure, and its numbers are written in scientific notation.

One mole (mol) is $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ particles (Avogadro's number, $N_A$), just as a dozen is 12. The number was chosen so that one mole of atoms has a mass in grams equal to the atomic mass in u: 1 mol of carbon atoms is 12.01 g, and 1 mol of iron atoms is 55.85 g.

An atomic mass unit is tiny: $1\ \text{u} \approx 1.66 \times 10^{-24}\ \text{g}$. If you take $6.022 \times 10^{23}$ atoms, each of mass $m$ u, the total is $m \times 1.66 \times 10^{-24} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}\ \text{g} \approx m\ \text{g}$, because those two numbers multiply to almost exactly 1. So the mole turns "u per atom" into "grams per mole" with the same number. Since 2019 the SI defines the mole by fixing $N_A$ at exactly $6.02214076 \times 10^{23}$; problems here round it to 6.022.

blocks.html: Thinking a mole of any substance has the same mass, or confusing a mole with a molecule. A mole is a count: a mole of iron and a mole of aluminum have the same number of atoms but different masses (55.85 g and 26.98 g), just as a dozen bowling balls outweighs a dozen golf balls.

How big is $6.022 \times 10^{23}$? Counting one atom per second, a mole would take about $1.9 \times 10^{16}$ years, more than a million times the age of the universe. Yet a mole of water is only 18 g, a little more than a tablespoon.

blocks.html: The Mole gave the mass of one mole of atoms. Compounds work the same way: a mole of molecules (or formula units) has a mass equal to the sum of its atoms' masses. Reading the formula correctly, including the parentheses of polyatomic ions, is the whole skill.

The molar mass of a substance (g/mol) is the sum of the atomic masses of all the atoms in its formula, each multiplied by how many times it appears. $$M(\mathrm{H_2O}) = 2(1.01) + 16.00 = 18.02\ \text{g/mol}.$$

One mole of $\mathrm{H_2O}$ molecules contains 2 mol of H atoms and 1 mol of O atoms. Their masses are $2 \times 1.01\ \text{g}$ and $16.00\ \text{g}$, so the mole of water weighs their sum. A subscript after parentheses multiplies everything inside: $\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2}$ contains 1 Ca, 2 N and 6 O.

blocks.html: With Molar Mass in hand, you can turn a mass you weigh into a number of moles, and moles into a number of particles. These are Dimensional Analysis problems with two new conversion factors.

Grams → moles: divide by the molar mass. Moles → grams: multiply by the molar mass. Moles → particles: multiply by $6.022 \times 10^{23}$. Moles are always in the middle: to go from grams to particles, pass through moles.

Molar mass is a rate: grams per mole. Written as a conversion factor it is either $\dfrac{18.02\ \text{g}}{1\ \text{mol}}$ or $\dfrac{1\ \text{mol}}{18.02\ \text{g}}$; pick the one that cancels the unit you have. Starting from grams, only $\dfrac{1\ \text{mol}}{18.02\ \text{g}}$ cancels grams, so you divide. Let the units decide, and the direction takes care of itself.

blocks.html: What fraction of a compound's mass comes from each element? Fertilizer bags, food labels and lab analyses all report this. You find it from the Molar Mass, using percents.

$$\%\ \text{of element} = \dfrac{(\text{number of its atoms in the formula}) \times (\text{its atomic mass})}{\text{molar mass of the compound}} \times 100\%.$$ The percents of all the elements add up to 100%.

One mole of the compound has a mass equal to its molar mass, and the formula says how much of that mass belongs to each element. Because every sample of a compound has the same makeup (Elements, Compounds and Mixtures), the same percent applies to a gram or a ton of it. Percent by mass uses masses, so heavy atoms count for more than light ones.

blocks.title: Carbon dioxide
blocks.q: What percent of the mass of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is carbon? (C 12.01, O 16.00)

blocks.title: Mass of an element in a sample
blocks.q: How many grams of iron are in $50.0\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$? (Fe 55.85, O 16.00)

blocks.html: Percent composition does not depend on the size of the sample: a gram or a ton of carbon dioxide is 27.29% carbon. That is why a measured percent can help identify a compound, and why it is the starting point for finding a formula in the next topic.

blocks.title: From lab data
blocks.q: Heating a $2.50\ \text{g}$ sample of a copper compound drives off everything but $1.27\ \text{g}$ of copper. What percent of the compound is copper?
steps: Percent by mass compares the part with the whole: $\dfrac{1.27\ \text{g}}{2.50\ \text{g}} \times 100\%$.
Comparing a measured percent with the percents calculated from possible formulas is one way chemists identify a compound.

blocks.html: Using the number of atoms instead of their masses, which would make water 67% hydrogen because 2 of its 3 atoms are hydrogen. By mass, water is only 11.2% hydrogen: $\dfrac{2(1.01)}{18.02} = 0.112$. Hydrogen atoms are numerous but light. Check that you multiplied each count by the atomic mass.

sources.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Section 3.2 Determining Empirical and Molecular Formulas

blocks.html: When chemists make or discover a new compound, one of the first measurements is how much of each element it contains. Percent Composition worked forward from a formula to percents. Here we work backward, from masses to the formula, using Grams, Moles and Particles and Equivalent Ratios and Ratio Tables.

The empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. 1. Take a 100 g sample, so each percent becomes grams. 2. Convert each mass to moles. 3. Divide every mole value by the smallest. 4. If the results are not all whole numbers, multiply them all by the same small number (×2 for 1.5, ×3 for 1.33 or 1.67, ×4 for 1.25).

Subscripts count atoms, and moles count atoms, so the formula is the ratio of moles, not of grams. Grams can't be compared directly because the atoms have different masses: 70 g of iron is far fewer atoms than 30 g of oxygen would suggest. Dividing by the smallest makes one element 1. A value like 1.5 is a real ratio (3 : 2), not rounding noise, so you scale up rather than round.

blocks.name: ratiotable
blocks.cap: Iron and oxygen atoms in the ratio 2 : 3. Move the marker to 1 Fe and read the O: 1.5. A ratio of 1 : 1.5 is the same as 2 : 3, so double everything.

blocks.title: Iron oxide
blocks.q: A compound is 69.94% iron and 30.06% oxygen by mass. Find its empirical formula. (Fe 55.85, O 16.00)
steps: In 100 g: 69.94 g Fe and 30.06 g O.
Divide by the smaller (1.252): Fe 1, O 1.500.
1.5 is not whole: multiply both by 2. Fe 2, O 3.

blocks.title: A hydrocarbon
blocks.q: A compound is 81.68% carbon and 18.32% hydrogen. Find its empirical formula. (C 12.01, H 1.01)

blocks.html: Rounding a ratio such as 1 : 1.5 to 1 : 2 instead of doubling it to 2 : 3, or using the mass ratio as if it were the mole ratio. Only round values that are within about 0.1 of a whole number. If you see .5, .33, .67 or .25, multiply. And always convert grams to moles before comparing.

blocks.html: The Empirical Formulas gives only a ratio. Formaldehyde ($\mathrm{CH_2O}$), acetic acid ($\mathrm{C_2H_4O_2}$) and glucose ($\mathrm{C_6H_{12}O_6}$) all have the same ratio, 1 C : 2 H : 1 O, yet they are very different substances. To tell them apart you need one more measurement: the molar mass.
The molecular formula is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula: $n = \dfrac{\text{molar mass}}{\text{empirical formula mass}}$. Multiply every subscript in the empirical formula by $n$.

A molecule is made of whole empirical-formula units: glucose is six $\mathrm{CH_2O}$ units bonded together. So its molar mass must be a whole number of times the empirical formula's mass. The molar mass can be measured separately (for example, with a mass spectrometer or from the behavior of the gas), and dividing tells you how many units are in one molecule.

blocks.title: Glucose
blocks.q: A compound has the empirical formula $\mathrm{CH_2O}$ and a molar mass of $180.18\ \text{g/mol}$. Find its molecular formula. (C 12.01, H 1.01, O 16.00)

blocks.title: Benzene
blocks.q: Benzene is 92.3% C and 7.7% H, with a molar mass of $78.11\ \text{g/mol}$. Find its molecular formula.
steps: Moles in 100 g: C $\dfrac{92.3}{12.01} = 7.69$; H $\dfrac{7.7}{1.01} = 7.62$. Ratio 1 : 1, so the empirical formula is CH.

blocks.title: Hydrogen peroxide
blocks.q: A compound has the empirical formula HO and a molar mass of $34.02\ \text{g/mol}$. What is its molecular formula?
steps: $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$, hydrogen peroxide, a different substance from water even though both contain only H and O.

blocks.html: Thinking the empirical formula is always the real formula, and giving glucose as $\mathrm{CH_2O}$. Sometimes $n = 1$ and the two match (water, $\mathrm{H_2O}$), but you can only know that from the molar mass. Check: the molar mass of your molecular formula must equal the measured molar mass.

sources.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Section 3.2 Determining Empirical and Molecular Formulas

blocks.html: In Physical and Chemical Changes you saw that a chemical change makes new substances. The atoms in those new substances are not new, though. A reaction pulls atoms away from their old partners and joins them to new ones. It never makes an atom and never destroys one.
In every chemical reaction the total mass of the reactants equals the total mass of the products. Atoms are only rearranged, so mass is conserved (the law of conservation of mass).

Count the atoms when methane burns: $$\mathrm{CH}_{4} + 2\mathrm{O}_{2} \to \mathrm{CO}_{2} + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$$ Before: 1 carbon, 4 hydrogen and 4 oxygen atoms. After: still 1 carbon, 4 hydrogen and 4 oxygen atoms, now in different molecules. Each kind of atom has the same mass wherever it ends up, so the same atoms always weigh the same. Antoine Lavoisier showed this in the 1770s and 1780s by weighing reactions carefully in sealed vessels.

blocks.name: ch-particles
blocks.cap: Two methane molecules burn. Press the regroup button and watch the atoms trade partners. The tally shows the same atoms of each element before and after.

blocks.title: Burning magnesium
blocks.q: A $2.43\ \text{g}$ strip of magnesium burns in air, and all of the white magnesium oxide that forms is kept. It weighs $4.03\ \text{g}$. What mass of oxygen joined the magnesium?
steps: The reaction is $2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O}_{2} \to 2\mathrm{MgO}$, so the reactants are magnesium and oxygen from the air.
$m = 4.03 - 2.43 = 1.60\ \text{g}$ of oxygen. The solid got heavier because oxygen atoms joined it.

blocks.title: A gas that escapes
blocks.q: Heating $10.00\ \text{g}$ of calcium carbonate breaks it down completely: $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3} \to \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO}_{2}$. The calcium oxide left in the dish weighs $5.60\ \text{g}$. What happened to the rest of the mass?
steps: The products are calcium oxide (a solid that stays) and carbon dioxide (a gas that drifts away).
The dish lost $4.40\ \text{g}$, but no mass was destroyed: it left as carbon dioxide gas.

blocks.html: Thinking mass is lost when wood burns or a gas fizzes away. The ash of a log weighs far less than the log, but most of the wood's atoms left as carbon dioxide and water vapor, joined by oxygen taken from the air. To check, ask: did a gas leave, or did a gas from the air join in? A balance only weighs the atoms that stay on it.
