OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 4.1 Writing and Balancing Chemical Equations

blocks.html: A chemical equation is a list of particles, written with formulas like the ones in Polyatomic Ions. Because atoms are conserved (Atoms Are Conserved), you will soon count atoms on both sides of an equation. Two kinds of numbers appear, and they mean very different things.

A subscript, the small number after a symbol, tells how many of that atom are in one molecule or formula unit; it is part of the substance's identity. A coefficient, the big number in front, tells how many molecules or formula units there are; it multiplies everything in the formula.

$\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ is water. $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{2}$ is hydrogen peroxide, a different substance with different properties. Changing a subscript changes what the substance is. A coefficient only counts copies: $3\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ is three water molecules, the way "3 bicycles" is still bicycles, just more of them.

blocks.name: ch-particles
blocks.cap: Left: $2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ is two separate water molecules. Right: $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{2}$ is one hydrogen peroxide molecule. Count the atoms: 4 H and 2 O on the left, 2 H and 2 O on the right.

items: Count the atoms in one formula unit first, using the subscripts.
A subscript after parentheses multiplies everything inside them: $\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$ has 1 Ca, 2 O and 2 H.
Then multiply every count by the coefficient.

blocks.title: Counting atoms in a coefficient
blocks.q: How many hydrogen and oxygen atoms are in $2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$?
steps: There are 2 molecules: $2 \times 2 = 4$ H atoms and $2 \times 1 = 2$ O atoms.
blocks.a: 4 hydrogen atoms and 2 oxygen atoms, in two separate molecules.

blocks.title: Parentheses and a coefficient
blocks.q: How many atoms of each element are in $3\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$?
steps: One $\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$: 1 Ca; the 2 after the parentheses doubles the OH group, so 2 O and 2 H.
Three formula units: Ca $3 \times 1 = 3$, O $3 \times 2 = 6$, H $3 \times 2 = 6$.

blocks.html: Reading $2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ as one molecule with four hydrogen atoms, or counting $3\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$ as 3 Ca, 1 O and 2 H. The coefficient counts whole molecules, and it multiplies every atom in the formula, including the ones inside parentheses. A quick check: draw the molecules as separate clumps and count.
This is why an equation can only be balanced with coefficients: they change how many molecules react without changing which substances they are. You will do that next in Balancing Equations.

sources.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 4.1 Writing and Balancing Chemical Equations

blocks.html: Atoms are conserved, so a correct equation has the same number of each kind of atom on both sides. A skeleton equation, with only the right formulas, usually does not. With Coefficients and Subscripts in hand, you can fix the count.
Balance an equation by changing coefficients, never subscripts, until every element has the same number of atoms on both sides. Use the smallest whole numbers.

The formulas are set by what the substances are: water is always $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$, because of how oxygen and hydrogen bond. The only freedom left is how many of each molecule take part, and that is exactly what a coefficient says.

blocks.name: ch-eqbalance
blocks.cap: Change the coefficients and watch the atom tally on each side. When every element matches, the equation is balanced.

items: Write correct formulas for every reactant and product.
Make a tally of each element on both sides.
Balance elements that appear in only one substance on each side first. Leave elements that appear alone, such as $\mathrm{O}_{2}$, $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ or a metal, for last.
Treat a polyatomic ion that appears unchanged on both sides as one unit.
If you need half a molecule, double every coefficient. Check the tally, and reduce if all coefficients share a factor.

blocks.title: Water from its elements
blocks.q: Balance $$\mathrm{H}_{2} + \mathrm{O}_{2} \to \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$$
steps: Tally: left 2 H, 2 O; right 2 H, 1 O. Oxygen is short on the right.
Put 2 in front of water: $2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ has 4 H and 2 O. Now hydrogen is short on the left.
Put 2 in front of $\mathrm{H}_{2}$: left 4 H, 2 O; right 4 H, 2 O.

blocks.title: Burning methane
blocks.q: Balance $$\mathrm{CH}_{4} + \mathrm{O}_{2} \to \mathrm{CO}_{2} + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$$
steps: Hydrogen: 4 on the left, so make $2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ (4 H).
Oxygen last: right side has $2 + 2 = 4$ O, so use $2\mathrm{O}_{2}$.

blocks.title: When a half shows up
blocks.q: Balance $$\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{6} + \mathrm{O}_{2} \to \mathrm{CO}_{2} + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$$
steps: Oxygen on the right: $2 \times 2 + 3 = 7$ atoms, which needs $\tfrac{7}{2}$ $\mathrm{O}_{2}$.
Double everything to clear the half: 2, 7, 4, 6.

blocks.html: Changing a subscript to make the numbers work, such as turning $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ into $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}_{2}$ so the oxygen balances. That turns water into hydrogen peroxide, so the equation now describes a different reaction. Check every formula at the end: is each one still the same substance you started with?

sources.name: OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 4.1 Writing and Balancing Chemical Equations

blocks.html: Thousands of reactions follow a handful of patterns. Once an equation is written and balanced, the pattern of who ends up with whom tells you its type, and knowing the types helps you predict products.

Five common types: synthesis (two or more substances join into one), decomposition (one substance breaks apart), single replacement (an element takes the place of another in a compound), double replacement (two compounds swap partners) and combustion (a fuel reacts with oxygen, giving carbon dioxide and water).

head: Type
Pattern
Example
blocks.cap: The five types and one example of each.

blocks.html: The types describe what happens to the partners. Atoms either join, split up, trade places one at a time or swap in pairs. Combustion gets its own name because it is so important: oxygen reacts with a fuel made of carbon and hydrogen, and a lot of energy comes out as heat and light.

blocks.name: ch-particles
blocks.cap: A decomposition: hydrogen peroxide molecules break apart into water and oxygen. One kind of reactant, two kinds of products.

blocks.title: A metal in an acid
blocks.q: Classify $$\mathrm{Zn} + 2\mathrm{HCl} \to \mathrm{ZnCl}_{2} + \mathrm{H}_{2}$$
steps: One reactant is an element (zinc) and one product is an element (hydrogen).
Zinc took hydrogen's place next to the chloride ions.

blocks.title: A fuel that contains oxygen
blocks.q: Classify $$\mathrm{C}_{2}\mathrm{H}_{5}\mathrm{OH} + 3\mathrm{O}_{2} \to 2\mathrm{CO}_{2} + 3\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$$
steps: Ethanol is a fuel made of carbon, hydrogen and some oxygen.
It reacts with $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ and gives only carbon dioxide and water.
blocks.a: Combustion. Oxygen inside the fuel does not change the type.

blocks.html: Sorting by surface pattern alone. "Two compounds react" does not always mean double replacement: $\mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} \to \mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_{2}$ makes one product, so it is synthesis, and $\mathrm{CH}_{4} + 2\mathrm{O}_{2} \to \mathrm{CO}_{2} + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ is combustion. And a fuel that contains oxygen, such as ethanol, still burns in combustion. Check the products: one product means synthesis; carbon dioxide and water from a fuel and oxygen means combustion.

Some reactions fit two types. Magnesium burning in oxygen is both a synthesis and a combustion, and an acid reacting with a hydroxide base is a double replacement that is also called a neutralization.

In Types of Reactions you met the single replacement pattern, A + BC → AC + B. It does not always happen: drop a copper wire into a zinc sulfate solution and nothing changes. Whether a metal can push another one out of a compound depends on which one gives up electrons more easily.

A metal replaces any metal below it in the activity series, and no metal above it. Metals above hydrogen also replace hydrogen in acids such as $\mathrm{HCl}$, giving hydrogen gas; copper, silver and gold do not.

Activity series, most active first: $$\mathrm{K} > \mathrm{Na} > \mathrm{Ca} > \mathrm{Mg} > \mathrm{Al} > \mathrm{Zn} > \mathrm{Fe} > \mathrm{Ni} > \mathrm{Sn} > \mathrm{Pb} > \mathrm{H} > \mathrm{Cu} > \mathrm{Ag} > \mathrm{Au}$$

Metal atoms react by losing electrons. When zinc sits in a solution of copper(II) ions, zinc atoms hand two electrons each to $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ ions: zinc dissolves as $\mathrm{Zn}^{2+}$, and copper metal coats the zinc. The reverse cannot happen on its own, because copper holds its electrons more tightly than zinc does. The activity series is simply the list of metals in order of how readily they give up electrons.

blocks.name: chem-activity
blocks.cap: Pick a metal and a solution. A metal above the dissolved metal (or above hydrogen, for the acid) reacts; one below it does not.

blocks.title: Iron in copper sulfate
blocks.q: Does iron react with copper(II) sulfate solution? If so, what forms?
steps: Iron is above copper in the series, so it can replace copper.
Iron forms $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ here, so with sulfate it makes $\mathrm{FeSO}_{4}$.
blocks.a: Yes: iron(II) sulfate and copper metal form.

blocks.title: Copper in zinc sulfate
blocks.q: Does copper react with zinc sulfate solution?
steps: Copper is below zinc in the series.
A less active metal cannot push a more active one out of its compound.

blocks.title: A metal in acid
blocks.q: What happens when magnesium is added to hydrochloric acid?
steps: Magnesium is above hydrogen, so it replaces the hydrogen in $\mathrm{HCl}$.
blocks.a: Hydrogen gas bubbles off and magnesium chloride stays in solution.

blocks.html: Thinking any metal can replace any other metal in a compound. Only a metal higher in the series can do it, and the switch never runs backward: since zinc replaces copper, copper cannot replace zinc. Check by finding both metals in the list before you write products.

A balanced equation is a recipe written in molecules. Since a mole is just a count of particles (Grams, Moles and Particles), the same recipe also works in moles, and you can scale it the way you solve a proportion.

The coefficients of a balanced equation give the mole ratio of every pair of substances. In $\mathrm{N}_{2} + 3\mathrm{H}_{2} \to 2\mathrm{NH}_{3}$, 1 mol of $\mathrm{N}_{2}$ reacts with 3 mol of $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ to make 2 mol of $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$. To convert, multiply by a ratio with the substance you want on top and the one you know on the bottom.

The equation says 1 molecule of $\mathrm{N}_{2}$ meets 3 molecules of $\mathrm{H}_{2}$. Multiply every count by $6.022 \times 10^{23}$, and you have 1 mole meeting 3 moles. Scaling a recipe up or down never changes its ratios, just as doubling a cookie recipe keeps two cups of flour for every cup of sugar.

blocks.name: ch-convert
blocks.cap: The mole map for the Haber process. The bridge between the two substances is always the mole ratio, $\tfrac{2\ \text{mol NH}_3}{3\ \text{mol H}_2}$ here.

blocks.title: Ammonia from hydrogen
blocks.q: How many moles of $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ form from $6.0\ \text{mol}$ of $\mathrm{H}_{2}$? $$\mathrm{N}_{2} + 3\mathrm{H}_{2} \to 2\mathrm{NH}_{3}$$
steps: The coefficients pair 3 mol $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ with 2 mol $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$.

blocks.title: Oxygen for a propane grill
blocks.q: How many moles of $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ are needed to burn $0.50\ \text{mol}$ of propane? $$\mathrm{C}_{3}\mathrm{H}_{8} + 5\mathrm{O}_{2} \to 3\mathrm{CO}_{2} + 4\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$$

blocks.html: Using the subscripts or the masses as the ratio. In $2\mathrm{H}_{2} + \mathrm{O}_{2} \to 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$, hydrogen and oxygen react 2 : 1 in moles; the 2 in $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ has nothing to do with it, and by mass the ratio is about 1 : 8. Check: the numbers in a mole ratio are always coefficients.
Every mole ratio comes from a balanced equation. If the equation is not balanced, the ratios are wrong, so balance first.

In the lab you weigh things in grams, but a balanced equation counts in moles. Mole Ratios crossed from one substance to another in moles; now add the two trips you learned in Grams, Moles and Particles, from grams into moles and back out.
Grams of A $\to$ moles of A (divide by A's molar mass) $\to$ moles of B (multiply by the mole ratio) $\to$ grams of B (multiply by B's molar mass).

Different molecules have different masses, so equal masses do not hold equal numbers of molecules. A gram of hydrogen holds about 16 times as many molecules as a gram of oxygen. The coefficients compare numbers of particles, so you must turn grams into moles before you use them, and turn back into grams only at the end.

blocks.name: ch-convert
blocks.cap: The full route from grams of hydrogen to grams of water: grams to moles, across the mole ratio, then moles to grams.

blocks.title: Water from hydrogen
blocks.q: How many grams of water form when $4.04\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ burns? $$2\mathrm{H}_{2} + \mathrm{O}_{2} \to 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$$ Molar masses: $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ 2.02 g/mol, $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ 18.02 g/mol.

blocks.title: Oxygen for propane
blocks.q: How many grams of $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ are needed to burn $22.0\ \text{g}$ of propane? $$\mathrm{C}_{3}\mathrm{H}_{8} + 5\mathrm{O}_{2} \to 3\mathrm{CO}_{2} + 4\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$$ Molar masses: $\mathrm{C}_{3}\mathrm{H}_{8}$ 44.11 g/mol, $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ 32.00 g/mol.

blocks.title: Working backward
blocks.q: How many grams of calcium carbonate must break down to make $10.0\ \text{g}$ of lime? $$\mathrm{CaCO}_{3} \to \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO}_{2}$$ Molar masses: $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$ 100.09 g/mol, $\mathrm{CaO}$ 56.08 g/mol.
steps: Start from what you know: $10.0 \div 56.08 = 0.1783\ \text{mol}$ of $\mathrm{CaO}$.

blocks.html: Applying the coefficients straight to grams, such as saying 4 g of hydrogen needs 2 g of oxygen because the equation says 2 : 1. Grams are not particles. Check with conservation of mass: $4.04\ \text{g}$ of hydrogen and the oxygen it uses must add up to the $36.0\ \text{g}$ of water, so the oxygen must be $32.0\ \text{g}$, not 2 g.
So far one reactant was given and the other was "in plenty". In a real mixture you have set amounts of both, and they rarely come in the exact ratio of the equation. One of them runs out first.

The limiting reactant is the one that runs out first; it alone decides how much product forms. To find it, change each amount to moles and divide by its coefficient: the smaller result is limiting. The other reactant is in excess, and some of it is left over.

Think of sandwiches that each need 2 slices of bread and 1 slice of cheese. With 10 slices of bread and 6 of cheese, the bread makes $10 \div 2 = 5$ sandwiches and the cheese could make 6. You run out of bread first, even though you have more bread than cheese. Dividing each amount by what one "unit" of the reaction needs is the fair comparison.

blocks.name: ch-limiting
blocks.cap: 3 molecules of nitrogen and 6 of hydrogen. Hydrogen is limiting even though there is more of it: each nitrogen needs three hydrogens.

blocks.title: Counting in moles
blocks.q: $3.0\ \text{mol}$ of $\mathrm{N}_{2}$ is mixed with $6.0\ \text{mol}$ of $\mathrm{H}_{2}$. $$\mathrm{N}_{2} + 3\mathrm{H}_{2} \to 2\mathrm{NH}_{3}$$ How much ammonia can form, and what is left over?
steps: Divide by the coefficients: $\mathrm{N}_{2}$ $3.0 \div 1 = 3.0$; $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ $6.0 \div 3 = 2.0$. Hydrogen is limiting.

blocks.title: Starting from grams
blocks.q: $10.0\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ and $64.0\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ react. $$2\mathrm{H}_{2} + \mathrm{O}_{2} \to 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$$ How many grams of water form? ($\mathrm{H}_{2}$ 2.02, $\mathrm{O}_{2}$ 32.00, $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ 18.02 g/mol)
steps: Divide by coefficients: $4.95 \div 2 = 2.48$ and $2.00 \div 1 = 2.00$. Oxygen is limiting, though its mass is larger.
Check: $4.00\ \text{mol}$ of $\mathrm{H}_{2}$ was used, so $0.95\ \text{mol}$ ($1.9\ \text{g}$) is left; $72.1 + 1.9 = 74.0\ \text{g}$, the mass you started with.

blocks.html: Picking the reactant with the smaller mass, or the smaller number of moles, without looking at the coefficients. In the second example oxygen has the larger mass and the smaller number of moles, and hydrogen has more moles but still is not limiting, because the reaction uses two of them for each $\mathrm{O}_{2}$. Always compare moles divided by coefficients.
The product amount you found in Limiting Reactant is the most a reaction can give. Real reactions almost always give less. A percent compares the two.

The theoretical yield is the amount of product the limiting reactant could make. The actual yield is what you collect. $$\text{percent yield} = \frac{\text{actual yield}}{\text{theoretical yield}} \times 100\%$$

Some reactant may not react, side reactions can make other products, and some product sticks to glassware or slips through a filter. All of these lower the actual yield, so the percent yield is normally below 100%. A result above 100% means something extra is being weighed, such as water left in a product that was not fully dried.

blocks.name: ch-limiting
blocks.cap: $28.0\ \text{g}$ of nitrogen with $8.0\ \text{g}$ of hydrogen: nitrogen is limiting, so it sets the theoretical yield. The bar for the actual yield shows how much was collected.

blocks.title: From the two yields
blocks.q: A reaction's theoretical yield of ammonia is $34.1\ \text{g}$. A student collects $30.0\ \text{g}$. What is the percent yield?

blocks.title: From a reactant mass
blocks.q: Heating $50.0\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$ gives $25.2\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{CaO}$. $$\mathrm{CaCO}_{3} \to \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO}_{2}$$ What is the percent yield? ($\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$ 100.09, $\mathrm{CaO}$ 56.08 g/mol)
steps: Theoretical yield: $50.0 \div 100.09 = 0.4996\ \text{mol}$ of $\mathrm{CaCO}_{3}$, which can make $0.4996\ \text{mol}$ of $\mathrm{CaO}$.

blocks.title: From a percent yield back to grams
blocks.q: A process makes ammonia with a $75\%$ yield. Its theoretical yield is $68.0\ \text{g}$. How many grams are actually collected?

blocks.html: Dividing the theoretical yield by the actual yield, which gives more than 100%, or working out the theoretical yield from the reactant in excess. Only the limiting reactant sets the theoretical yield. Check: the actual yield goes on top, and a percent yield above 100% is a warning sign.

In Pressure you met pressure as force spread over an area, $P = F/A$. In Solids, Liquids and Gases you saw that gas particles fly about freely. Put the two together and you can see where a gas's pressure comes from.

Gas pressure is the push of particles colliding with the walls, per unit of wall area. It acts equally in every direction. Common units: $$1\ \text{atm} = 101.325\ \text{kPa} = 760\ \text{mmHg} = 760\ \text{torr}$$

Every particle that bounces off a wall gives it a tiny push. Billions of billions of collisions each second blend into a steady force. Because the particles move in every direction at random, the top, the bottom and the sides are all hit equally often, which is why a balloon swells into a round shape. More particles, or faster ones, mean more collisions and harder ones: more pressure.

blocks.html: Air pressure at sea level holds up a column of mercury about 760 mm tall in a barometer, which is where the unit mmHg comes from. Using the equalities as conversion factors (Dimensional Analysis) turns one unit into another.

steps: Less than 760: there is less air pushing down from above.

blocks.html: Thinking gas pressure pushes only downward, or that gas particles settle at the bottom of their container like sand. Gas particles are far apart and keep moving, so they fill the whole container and hit every wall. Check with something you know: a sealed balloon bulges out evenly in all directions.
Try it in Gas in a Box: count the wall hits each second, then add particles or warm the gas and watch the pressure follow.

Gas Pressure pictured pressure as particle collisions. The kinetic molecular theory turns that picture into a short list of ideas that explains every gas law to come. It also gives the kelvin scale of Temperature Scales and Absolute Zero its meaning.

items: A gas is made of particles that are tiny compared with the distances between them, so a gas is mostly empty space.
The particles move fast, in straight lines, in random directions, until they collide.
Collisions with each other and with the walls lose no energy overall.
In an ideal gas the particles do not attract or repel each other.
The average kinetic energy of the particles is proportional to the kelvin temperature.

blocks.html: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles: double the kelvin temperature and the average kinetic energy doubles. At any temperature the particles have a wide spread of speeds.

Collisions trade energy back and forth, so at any moment some particles are slow and some are very fast; only the average is fixed by the temperature. The ideas explain gas behavior: empty space makes gases easy to squeeze, random motion makes them spread out and mix, and collisions make pressure. Because kinetic energy is $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, lighter particles at the same temperature must move faster to have the same average energy.

steps: Dividing the Celsius numbers, $327 \div 27 \approx 12$, would be far off.

blocks.title: Light and heavy particles
blocks.q: Helium and nitrogen are both at $300\ \text{K}$. Compare their average kinetic energies and their average speeds.
steps: Same temperature, so the same average kinetic energy.
A helium atom ($4\ \text{g/mol}$) is much lighter than a nitrogen molecule ($28\ \text{g/mol}$), so it must move faster to carry the same $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.
blocks.a: Equal average kinetic energies; helium atoms move faster on average.

blocks.html: Thinking every particle in a gas moves at the same speed, or that particles stop moving at $0^\circ\text{C}$. Temperature fixes only the average, and the curve above shows the wide spread. And $0^\circ\text{C}$ is $273\ \text{K}$, far above absolute zero: water freezes there, but gas particles keep moving.
Explore it in Gas in a Box: turn on the speed histogram, then change the temperature.

Squeeze a sealed syringe of air and it pushes back harder. Kinetic Molecular Theory explains why, and Solving for a Variable lets you turn the rule into an equation you can solve for any one quantity.
At constant temperature, for a fixed amount of gas, pressure and volume are inversely proportional: $$P_1V_1 = P_2V_2$$ Halve the volume and the pressure doubles.

Push the same particles into half the space and each one reaches a wall twice as often. Twice the collisions per second means twice the pressure. The particles keep the same speeds, because the temperature has not changed; only the crowding changes.

blocks.title: Squeezing a cylinder
blocks.q: A gas in a cylinder has a volume of $6.0\ \text{L}$ at $1.0\ \text{atm}$. At constant temperature it is squeezed to $2.0\ \text{L}$. What is the new pressure?
steps: $P_2 = 3.0\ \text{atm}$: one third of the volume, three times the pressure.

blocks.title: A syringe that expands
blocks.q: A sealed syringe holds $250\ \text{mL}$ of air at $760\ \text{mmHg}$. The outside pressure drops to $380\ \text{mmHg}$, at constant temperature. What volume does the air take up?
steps: $$V_2 = \dfrac{P_1V_1}{P_2} = \dfrac{760\ \text{mmHg} \times 250\ \text{mL}}{380\ \text{mmHg}}$$ The pressure units cancel, so no conversion is needed.
$V_2 = 500\ \text{mL}$: half the pressure, twice the volume.

blocks.html: Expecting every gas relation to be direct, so that more pressure means more volume. For Boyle's law it is the opposite. Check the direction of your answer: if the gas was squeezed, its pressure must have gone up; if it expanded, the pressure must have gone down.

You can see the law in everyday life: a sealed bag of chips puffs up on a mountain road, because the outside pressure is lower there. Try it in Gas in a Box by moving the piston with the temperature locked.

blocks.html: A balloon taken from a warm room into the cold shrinks. Kinetic Molecular Theory explains it, and the relation turns out to be a proportional one, as long as temperature is measured from absolute zero.
At constant pressure, for a fixed amount of gas, volume is proportional to the kelvin temperature: $$\frac{V_1}{T_1} = \frac{V_2}{T_2}$$

Warmer particles move faster, so they hit the walls harder and more often. If the container can grow, like a balloon or a free piston, it expands until the pressure inside again matches the pressure outside. Measured carefully, the volume of every gas shrinks along a straight line that would reach zero at $-273.15^\circ\text{C}$. That point is absolute zero, and it is why the gas laws only work in kelvins.

blocks.html: Using Celsius temperatures in the ratio. Warming from $10^\circ\text{C}$ to $20^\circ\text{C}$ does not double the volume: in kelvins it is $283.15$ to $293.15$, a rise of only 3.5%. Check: if the temperatures you divide could be zero or negative, they are not in kelvins.
Try it in Gas in a Box: let the piston float, heat the gas, and read the volume against the kelvin temperature.

blocks.html: Boyle's Law held the temperature constant and Charles's Law held the pressure constant. Hold the volume constant instead, as in a rigid steel tank, and you get the third law. Then all three fit into one equation.

At constant volume, pressure is proportional to kelvin temperature (Gay-Lussac's law): $\dfrac{P_1}{T_1} = \dfrac{P_2}{T_2}$. For a fixed amount of gas, all three laws combine into $$\frac{P_1V_1}{T_1} = \frac{P_2V_2}{T_2}$$

In a rigid tank the walls cannot move, so when the particles speed up they simply hit harder and more often: pressure rises in proportion to the kelvin temperature. In general, $PV/T$ stays the same for a fixed amount of gas. Set $T_1 = T_2$ and the combined law becomes Boyle's law; set $P_1 = P_2$ and it becomes Charles's law; set $V_1 = V_2$ and it becomes Gay-Lussac's law.

Then check each factor's direction: a drop in pressure should make the volume bigger, a drop in temperature smaller.

blocks.html: The Gay-Lussac's Law and the Combined Gas Law kept the amount of gas fixed. Now let the amount change. Counting it in moles (Grams, Moles and Particles) leads to one of the most useful facts about gases.

At the same temperature and pressure, equal volumes of gases contain equal numbers of particles (Avogadro's law): $\dfrac{V_1}{n_1} = \dfrac{V_2}{n_2}$. At $0^\circ\text{C}$ and $1\ \text{atm}$, which this course calls STP, one mole of any gas occupies $22.4\ \text{L}$.

A gas is mostly empty space: the particles take up a tiny fraction of the volume, and in an ideal gas they hardly pull on each other. So the volume depends on how many particles are bouncing around and how hard they hit, not on how big or heavy each one is. A heavy $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ molecule moves more slowly than a light helium atom, but it hits just as hard on average, because both have the same average kinetic energy at the same temperature.

blocks.cap: At the same temperature and pressure, a liter of helium and a liter of carbon dioxide hold the same number of particles, even though each $\mathrm{CO}_{2}$ molecule has 11 times the mass of a helium atom.

Some books define STP as $0^\circ\text{C}$ and $1\ \text{bar}$ (IUPAC's choice since 1982), where a mole of gas takes up $22.7\ \text{L}$. This course uses $0^\circ\text{C}$ and $1\ \text{atm}$ with $22.4\ \text{L}$. Try adding gas at constant pressure in Gas in a Box.

blocks.html: Boyle, Charles and Avogadro each described one relation with the rest held still. Together they say that a gas's volume grows with moles and temperature and shrinks with pressure. One equation holds all of it.
$$PV = nRT$$ with $P$ the pressure, $V$ the volume in liters, $n$ the moles and $T$ the kelvin temperature. The gas constant $R$ must match the pressure unit.

head: Pressure unit
R
blocks.cap: The same constant in three sets of units.

blocks.html: From the separate laws, $V$ is proportional to $nT/P$. A proportion becomes an equation with a constant: $V = R\,nT/P$, or $PV = nRT$. Check it against Avogadro: for $1\ \text{mol}$ at $273.15\ \text{K}$ and $1\ \text{atm}$, $V = 0.08206 \times 273.15 = 22.4\ \text{L}$. And if the amount of gas is fixed, $PV/T = nR$ is constant, which is the combined gas law.

"Ideal" means the particles are treated as points that never attract each other. Real gases follow $PV = nRT$ closely at ordinary conditions and stray from it at high pressure and low temperature. Experiment with all the variables in Gas in a Box.

blocks.html: Stir salt or sugar into water and it vanishes from sight. Nothing has been destroyed: the forces from Intermolecular Forces and the ions of Ionic Bonds explain exactly where the particles went.

Water molecules are polar. Their partly charged ends pull ions and polar molecules away from a solid and surround them, so the solute spreads evenly through the water. Ionic compounds dissolve as separate ions; molecular compounds such as sugar dissolve as whole molecules. Like dissolves like: polar and ionic solutes dissolve in polar solvents, and nonpolar solutes in nonpolar solvents.

A solid dissolves when its particles are attracted to the solvent about as strongly as they are attracted to each other. In salt water, the slightly negative oxygen ends of water molecules face each $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ and the slightly positive hydrogen ends face each $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$; these attractions pull ions off the crystal one by one. Oil does not dissolve because water molecules attract each other (through hydrogen bonds) much more strongly than they attract oil, so they squeeze the oil out.

blocks.cap: Left: a crystal of salt comes apart into $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$ ions, each wrapped in water molecules. Right: sugar molecules spread out, but each stays one whole molecule.

blocks.name: ch-imf

blocks.title: Counting ions
blocks.q: $0.50\ \text{mol}$ of calcium chloride, $\mathrm{CaCl}_{2}$, dissolves in water. How many moles of ions are in the solution?
steps: Each formula unit splits into one $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ and two $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$: $$\mathrm{CaCl}_{2} \to \mathrm{Ca}^{2+} + 2\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$$
$0.50\ \text{mol}$ of $\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}$ and $1.00\ \text{mol}$ of $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$: $1.5\ \text{mol}$ of ions in all.

blocks.title: Nothing disappears
blocks.q: $10.0\ \text{g}$ of sugar dissolves in $100.0\ \text{g}$ of water. What is the mass of the solution?
steps: Every sugar molecule is still there, spread among the water molecules.

blocks.html: Thinking dissolved sugar has disappeared or turned into water, or that dissolving is the same as melting. The solution tastes sweet and weighs more, so the sugar is still there. And sugar dissolves in water at room temperature, far below its melting point: melting needs heat and no second substance, while dissolving needs a solvent to pull the particles apart.
There is a limit to Why Things Dissolve: keep adding sugar to tea and some eventually stays at the bottom. That limit depends on the solute, the solvent and the temperature.

The solubility of a substance is the most that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature, often stated in grams per 100 g of water. On a solubility curve, a point on the curve is saturated, below it unsaturated (more can dissolve), and above it supersaturated (an unstable state that crystallizes easily).

In a saturated solution, particles keep leaving the solid and returning to it at equal rates, so the amount dissolved stays at the limit. For most solids, warmer water dissolves more, because faster-moving water molecules pull particles off the crystal more readily, but the size of the effect varies a lot. Gases are the other way around: dissolved gas particles that gain energy escape from the liquid, so warm water holds less gas.

blocks.html: Thinking every solute, gases included, dissolves better in hotter water, or calling any solution with a lot of solute "saturated". Saturated means at the limit for that temperature, whatever the amount: a solution with only $7.3\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{KClO}_{3}$ per 100 g of water at $20^\circ\text{C}$ is already saturated. Check the curve for that substance at that temperature.

blocks.html: To use a solution in a reaction, you need to know how many moles of solute a given volume holds. Molarity is a Unit Rates that says exactly that, built from moles and the solutions you have met.
$$\text{molarity } (M) = \frac{\text{moles of solute}}{\text{liters of solution}}$$ A $0.40\ \text{M}$ (read "0.40 molar") solution holds $0.40\ \text{mol}$ of solute in each liter of solution.

Like miles per hour, molarity is a rate you can run forward or backward: moles $= M \times V$, and $V = \text{moles} / M$. That lets you measure out moles of a dissolved substance with a graduated cylinder or a pipet instead of a balance. The volume is of the whole solution, because that is what you measure and pour.

blocks.title: Moles and liters
blocks.q: $0.20\ \text{mol}$ of NaCl is dissolved in enough water to make $0.50\ \text{L}$ of solution. What is the molarity?
steps: Each liter of the solution holds $0.40\ \text{mol}$ of NaCl.

blocks.html: Dividing by the volume of water added instead of the final volume of solution, or putting milliliters into the formula as if they were liters. Dissolving $13.5\ \text{g}$ of glucose in $500\ \text{mL}$ of water gives a little more than $500\ \text{mL}$ of solution, so the concentration comes out a bit low. Check that the volume is in liters and is the volume of the finished solution.
Labs keep concentrated "stock" solutions and dilute them as needed. Molarity tells you what happens to the concentration when you add water.

Adding water spreads the same moles of solute through more volume. Since moles $= MV$ stays the same, $$M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$$ where 1 is before and 2 is after diluting. Any volume unit works, as long as both volumes use the same one.
Water adds volume but no solute. The moles of solute before, $M_1V_1$, must equal the moles after, $M_2V_2$. Double the volume and every liter holds half as much solute, so the molarity halves.

blocks.title: Using a stock solution
blocks.q: How much $6.00\ \text{M}$ stock solution is needed to make $500.\ \text{mL}$ of $0.300\ \text{M}$ solution?
steps: Measure $25.0\ \text{mL}$ of stock and add water until the total volume is $500.\ \text{mL}$ (that is, about $475\ \text{mL}$ of water).

steps: The formula gives the total volume; subtract what you started with.

blocks.html: Thinking that adding water changes the number of moles of solute. It changes only the volume, and so the concentration. Check: $M_1V_1$ and $M_2V_2$ should come out equal, and a diluted solution must always have a lower molarity than the one you started with.

Diluting is how one concentrated stock bottle can supply many weaker solutions, and how very weak solutions are made accurately: diluting 10 times, and then 10 times again, gives a solution 100 times weaker without measuring a tiny volume.

Mix two clear solutions and a cloudy solid may suddenly appear. This is a double replacement from Types of Reactions, and whether it happens depends on what dissolves. Writing the solid's formula uses the ion charges of Polyatomic Ions.

When two solutions of ionic compounds mix, the ions can pair up in new ways. If one of the new combinations is insoluble, it comes out of solution as a solid, the precipitate. The solubility rules predict when this happens.

blocks.html: In solution, every ion is surrounded by water molecules. Some pairs of ions, such as $\mathrm{Ag}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$, attract each other in a crystal more strongly than water can hold them apart. When those two ions meet, they lock into a solid and settle out, while the other ions, the spectators, stay dissolved.

blocks.name: ch-particles
blocks.cap: Silver nitrate solution meets sodium chloride solution. Silver and chloride ions lock together as solid $\mathrm{AgCl}$; the ringed $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{NO}_{3}^{-}$ ions are spectators.

blocks.title: Silver chloride
blocks.q: What forms when silver nitrate and sodium chloride solutions are mixed?
steps: Swap partners: the new pairs are $\mathrm{AgCl}$ and $\mathrm{NaNO}_{3}$.
Sodium and nitrate compounds are soluble; silver chloride is not.

blocks.title: Lead iodide
blocks.q: Solutions of $\mathrm{Pb}(\mathrm{NO}_{3})_{2}$ and $\mathrm{KI}$ are mixed. What is the precipitate, and what is the balanced equation?
steps: New pairs: lead with iodide, and potassium with nitrate. Lead(II) iodide is insoluble.
Charges: $\mathrm{Pb}^{2+}$ needs two $\mathrm{I}^{-}$, so the formula is $\mathrm{PbI}_{2}$.

blocks.title: No reaction
blocks.q: Solutions of $\mathrm{KNO}_{3}$ and $\mathrm{NaCl}$ are mixed. Does a precipitate form?
steps: Both are soluble (potassium, sodium and nitrate compounds always are).
blocks.a: No: the ions simply stay mixed in solution.

blocks.html: Thinking every ionic compound dissolves in water, or writing a precipitate whose charges do not balance, such as "PbI" instead of $\mathrm{PbI}_{2}$. Check the rules for each new pair, and build each formula from the ion charges so that the total charge is zero.
Many compounds change water in a special way when they dissolve: they add hydrogen ions or hydroxide ions (OH⁻). That one change explains why lemon juice is sour and why soap feels slippery.

In water, an acid makes hydronium ions, $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$, and a base makes hydroxide ions, $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$. (Chemists often write $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ as shorthand for $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$.)

A molecule of hydrogen chloride hands its hydrogen nucleus, an $\mathrm{H}^{+}$, to a water molecule: $$\mathrm{HCl} + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} \to \mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+} + \mathrm{Cl}^{-}$$ Sodium hydroxide is made of $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ ions and simply releases its $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ when it dissolves. Ammonia has no OH at all, yet it is a base: it takes an $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ from water and leaves $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ behind. What matters is what a substance does in water, not which letters are in its formula.

items: Acids: sour foods such as lemon juice and vinegar contain them; they turn blue litmus paper red and react with many metals, giving hydrogen gas.
Bases: soap and household ammonia are basic; they feel slippery and turn red litmus paper blue.

blocks.title: Nitric acid
blocks.q: What does nitric acid, $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$, do in water?
steps: It gives its $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ to a water molecule: $$\mathrm{HNO}_{3} + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} \to \mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+} + \mathrm{NO}_{3}^{-}$$
It makes $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$, so it is an acid.
blocks.a: An acid: it makes hydronium and nitrate ions.

blocks.title: Methanol
blocks.q: Methanol, $\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{OH}$, has an OH group. Is it a base?
steps: Its OH is held to carbon by a covalent bond, which does not break when methanol dissolves.
Methanol dissolves as whole molecules and adds no $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ and no $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$.
blocks.a: Neither an acid nor a base.

blocks.html: Deciding from the formula alone: calling any compound with H an acid (methane, $\mathrm{CH}_{4}$, is not one) or any compound with OH a base (the alcohol $\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{OH}$ is not one). Ask what the substance does in water: does it make $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$, $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$, or neither?
Test kitchen liquids with indicators in Mixing Lab, where nothing can spill.

blocks.html: The water-based definitions work well, but they hide what actually moves. In every acid–base reaction, a hydrogen ion, a bare proton, passes from one particle to another.

A Brønsted–Lowry acid donates an $\mathrm{H}^{+}$; a base accepts one. After the transfer, the acid has become its conjugate base (one H and one positive charge fewer) and the base has become its conjugate acid (one H and one positive charge more).

An $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ is just a proton, with no electrons of its own. It can only attach to a particle that offers a pair of electrons to bond with, a lone pair. That is what a base has: the nitrogen in ammonia and the oxygen in water each have a lone pair to accept a proton. Water can also give up a proton, so it can act as an acid or as a base, depending on its partner.

blocks.name: ch-lewis
blocks.cap: Ammonia uses its lone pair to bond to an incoming $\mathrm{H}^{+}$, becoming ammonium, $\mathrm{NH}_{4}^{+}$. The base is the electron-pair side of the new bond.

blocks.title: Hydrofluoric acid and water
blocks.q: Label the acid, base and conjugates in $$\mathrm{HF} + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{F}^{-} + \mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$$
steps: $\mathrm{HF}$ loses an $\mathrm{H}^{+}$: it is the acid, and $\mathrm{F}^{-}$ is its conjugate base.
$\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ gains the $\mathrm{H}^{+}$: it is the base, and $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$ is its conjugate acid.
blocks.a: Acid $\mathrm{HF}$ / conjugate base $\mathrm{F}^{-}$; base $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ / conjugate acid $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$.

blocks.title: Water as an acid
blocks.q: Label the acid and base in $$\mathrm{NH}_{3} + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{NH}_{4}^{+} + \mathrm{OH}^{-}$$
steps: $\mathrm{NH}_{3}$ gains an $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ to become $\mathrm{NH}_{4}^{+}$: it is the base.
$\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$ loses an $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ to become $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$: here water is the acid.

blocks.title: Writing conjugates
blocks.q: Write the conjugate base of $\mathrm{HSO}_{4}^{-}$ and the conjugate acid of $\mathrm{CO}_{3}^{2-}$.
steps: Conjugate base: remove one $\mathrm{H}^{+}$. $\mathrm{HSO}_{4}^{-}$ becomes $\mathrm{SO}_{4}^{2-}$ (one less H, charge one lower).
Conjugate acid: add one $\mathrm{H}^{+}$. $\mathrm{CO}_{3}^{2-}$ becomes $\mathrm{HCO}_{3}^{-}$ (one more H, charge one higher).

blocks.html: Building a conjugate base by removing OH instead of one $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ (the conjugate base of $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$ is $\mathrm{NO}_{3}^{-}$, not $\mathrm{NO}_{2}^{+}$), or thinking water can never act as an acid or a base. Check that the pair differs by exactly one H and that the charge changed by exactly 1.

blocks.html: Acids raise the amount of $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$ in water. That amount ranges from about $1\ \text{mol/L}$ down to $0.00000000000001\ \text{mol/L}$, so chemists count it in powers of ten, using the negative exponents you already know.

If $[\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}] = 1 \times 10^{-n}\ \text{M}$, the pH is $n$. Each step of 1 on the pH scale is a factor of 10 in $[\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}]$. At $25^\circ\text{C}$, pH 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic and above 7 is basic.

Square brackets mean "concentration in mol/L". Writing the exponent instead of the whole number squeezes a huge range into a short scale from about 0 to 14. The price is that the scale is not even: going from pH 4 to pH 3 means ten times as much $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$, and from pH 4 to pH 2 means a hundred times as much.

blocks.name: ch-phscale
blocks.cap: Move the pointer along the scale. The concentration of $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$ changes tenfold with every step, and everyday liquids sit at their measured pH values.

head: Liquid
Typical pH
blocks.cap: Measured pH values (U.S. FDA food pH table; OpenStax Chemistry 2e, 14.2), as on Mixing Lab.

blocks.title: From concentration to pH
blocks.q: A solution has $[\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}] = 1 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{M}$. What is its pH?
steps: The exponent is $-4$, so the pH is 4.

blocks.title: How many times more?
blocks.q: How many times more $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$ is in a solution at pH 3 than in one at pH 5?
steps: Each step is a factor of 10: $10 \times 10 = 10^2 = 100$.

blocks.title: Diluting a strong acid
blocks.q: $0.001\ \text{M}$ hydrochloric acid gives all of its $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ to water. What is its pH, and what is the pH after diluting it to 10 times its volume?

blocks.html: Thinking pH 3 is only a little more acidic than pH 4. It has 10 times the $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$; pH 3 against pH 6 is 1,000 times. Check by writing both concentrations as powers of ten and dividing.
Test kitchen liquids against the scale in Mixing Lab.

sources.name: U.S. Food and Drug Administration, approximate pH of foods (as cited on Mixing Lab)

blocks.html: The The pH Scale tracked $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$. What about $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$? In water the two are tied together, and multiplying powers of ten (Multiplying Powers) shows how.

In every water solution at $25^\circ\text{C}$: $$[\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}][\mathrm{OH}^{-}] = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}$$ Defining pOH like pH (the power of ten of $[\mathrm{OH}^{-}]$), this means $\text{pH} + \text{pOH} = 14$.

Water molecules trade protons with each other all the time: $$2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+} + \mathrm{OH}^{-}$$ In pure water this gives $1.0 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{M}$ of each ion, and their product is $10^{-7} \times 10^{-7} = 10^{-14}$. Add an acid and the extra $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$ reacts with some $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$, so $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ drops until the product is back at $10^{-14}$. Adding a base works the other way. One goes up, the other comes down.

blocks.name: ch-phscale
blocks.cap: Both concentrations shown together: as the pointer moves, $[\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}]$ and $[\mathrm{OH}^{-}]$ change in opposite directions, and pH plus pOH always makes 14.

blocks.title: From one ion to the other
blocks.q: A solution has $[\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}] = 1.0 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{M}$. Find $[\mathrm{OH}^{-}]$ and the pOH.

blocks.title: A coefficient other than 1
blocks.q: A solution has $[\mathrm{OH}^{-}] = 2.0 \times 10^{-4}\ \text{M}$. What is $[\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}]$?
steps: Divide the numbers and subtract the exponents: $0.50 \times 10^{-10} = 5.0 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{M}$.

blocks.html: Thinking a basic solution has no $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$ at all, or that pure water contains no ions. Every water solution has both ions; their product is fixed at $1.0 \times 10^{-14}$, so neither can ever reach zero. A basic solution just has more $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ than $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$.
The value $1.0 \times 10^{-14}$ holds at $25^\circ\text{C}$. It grows as water warms, so the neutral point shifts a little; pH of Strong Acids and Bases works with that.
Two acids at the same concentration can have very different pH values. The reason is how completely each one gives up its protons, the proton transfer you met earlier, measured on the The pH Scale.

A strong acid ionizes completely in water: every molecule gives its $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ to water. A weak acid ionizes only partly; most of its molecules stay whole. The common strong acids are $\mathrm{HCl}$, $\mathrm{HBr}$, $\mathrm{HI}$, $\mathrm{HNO}_{3}$, $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}$ (its first H) and $\mathrm{HClO}_{4}$; most other acids, such as acetic acid, are weak.

For a weak acid, the reverse reaction competes: the conjugate base keeps grabbing protons back, $$\mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COOH} + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CH}_{3}\mathrm{COO}^{-} + \mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$$ so at any moment only a small fraction of the molecules are ionized. For a strong acid the conjugate base, such as $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$, has almost no pull on a proton, so the reaction runs essentially all the way.

blocks.name: ch-particles
blocks.cap: The same number of acid molecules in each box. Every HCl has ionized; only a few acetic acid molecules have.

blocks.title: A strong acid
blocks.q: What is $[\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}]$ in $0.10\ \text{M}$ HCl?
steps: HCl is strong: every molecule makes one $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$.

blocks.title: A weak acid
blocks.q: In $0.10\ \text{M}$ acetic acid, about $1.3\%$ of the molecules are ionized. What is $[\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}]$?
steps: That is less than one seventy-fifth of the strong acid's value at the same concentration, so the pH is near 2.9, not 1.

blocks.title: Strength against concentration
blocks.q: Which has more $\mathrm{H}_{3}\mathrm{O}^{+}$: $0.0010\ \text{M}$ HCl, or vinegar, about $0.83\ \text{M}$ acetic acid with $0.47\%$ of its molecules ionized?
blocks.a: The vinegar: a concentrated weak acid can beat a dilute strong one.

blocks.html: Confusing a strong acid with a concentrated one, and a weak acid with a dilute one. Strength is how completely the acid ionizes; concentration is how much acid is in each liter. Check by asking two separate questions: what fraction ionizes, and how many moles per liter are there?

blocks.html: Mix a strong acid with a hydroxide base and the two cancel each other's effects. Writing it as a balanced equation shows what is left.

An acid and a hydroxide base react to make water and a salt: $$\mathrm{HCl} + \mathrm{NaOH} \to \mathrm{NaCl} + \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$$ The heart of every such reaction is $\mathrm{H}^{+} + \mathrm{OH}^{-} \to \mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$. The salt is the ionic compound made of the base's cation and the acid's anion.

Hydrogen ions and hydroxide ions attract each other strongly and join into water molecules, releasing heat. The other ions, such as $\mathrm{Na}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl}^{-}$, do not react; they are left in solution as the salt. If the acid gives two $\mathrm{H}^{+}$, like $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}$, it needs two $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$, which sets the coefficients.

blocks.name: ch-titration
blocks.cap: Adding NaOH to $25.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.100\ \text{M}$ HCl. The pH reaches 7 only when the moles of base equal the moles of acid; before that the mixture is acidic, after it basic.

blocks.title: A salt from a diprotic acid
blocks.q: Write the balanced equation for sulfuric acid and potassium hydroxide, and find the moles of KOH that neutralize $0.15\ \text{mol}$ of $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}$.
steps: Each $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}$ gives two $\mathrm{H}^{+}$, and each KOH gives one $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$: $$\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4} + 2\mathrm{KOH} \to \mathrm{K}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4} + 2\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$$

blocks.title: Unequal amounts
blocks.q: $0.10\ \text{mol}$ of HCl is mixed with $0.05\ \text{mol}$ of NaOH. Is the result acidic, basic or neutral?

blocks.html: Thinking that mixing any acid with any base gives pH 7. That happens only when the moles of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ and $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ match exactly (and, as you will see later, only for a strong acid with a strong base). Check by comparing moles, not volumes or names.
Neutralize an acid drop by drop in Mixing Lab.
Neutralization becomes a measuring tool when one of the solutions has a known Molarity. A titration counts the moles of an unknown acid by finding exactly how much base it takes, using a mole ratio.

In a titration, base of known molarity is added from a buret until it has exactly used up the acid: the equivalence point, shown by an indicator's color change. Then moles of base $= M_b V_b$, the mole ratio gives moles of acid, and $M_a = \text{moles of acid} / V_a$.

Molarity times volume counts moles, so reading a buret is a way to count particles. At the equivalence point, the moles of $\mathrm{OH}^{-}$ added match the moles of $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ the acid can give. For an acid with one $\mathrm{H}^{+}$ that means equal moles; for $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}$, with two, the base needed is twice the moles of acid.

blocks.name: ch-titration
blocks.cap: A titration curve. The pH rises slowly, then jumps steeply at the equivalence point, where the indicator changes color. Drag to add base.

blocks.title: Finding a concentration
blocks.q: A $25.0\ \text{mL}$ sample of HCl needs $18.6\ \text{mL}$ of $0.100\ \text{M}$ NaOH to reach the endpoint. What is the molarity of the acid?
steps: HCl and NaOH react 1 : 1, so moles of HCl $= 1.86 \times 10^{-3}$.

blocks.title: An acid with two protons
blocks.q: $20.0\ \text{mL}$ of $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}$ needs $24.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.150\ \text{M}$ NaOH. What is the molarity of the acid?

blocks.title: How much base?
blocks.q: What volume of $0.100\ \text{M}$ NaOH reaches the equivalence point with $25.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.0800\ \text{M}$ $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}$?

blocks.html: Using $M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$ for an acid such as $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{SO}_{4}$ that gives two $\mathrm{H}^{+}$. That shortcut assumes a 1 : 1 ratio, so it gives twice the true acid concentration here. Always go through moles and the mole ratio from the balanced equation.
For a weak acid titrated with a strong base, the equivalence point lies above pH 7; Weak Acid–Strong Base Titration Curves explains why. Titrate drop by drop in Mixing Lab.

In Solids, Liquids and Gases you saw that particles never stop moving, and Temperature Scales and Absolute Zero gave you kelvins. Heat and temperature both describe that motion, but they are not the same thing.

Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the particles in a sample. Thermal energy is the total energy of their motion, so it also depends on how much material there is. Heat is energy that flows from a hotter object to a colder one because of their temperature difference, until they reach the same temperature (thermal equilibrium).

Where a hot object touches a cold one, its fast particles bump into slower ones and, on average, pass energy to them. The reverse bumps also happen, but less energy goes that way, so the net flow is always from hot to cold. The flow stops when the averages match. Nothing called "cold" ever flows: a cold object only takes in less energy than it gives off, or gains energy from you.

blocks.name: ch-calorimeter
blocks.cap: Two copper blocks touching. Heat flows from the hot block to the cool one until both reach the same temperature; the energy one block loses is the energy the other gains.

blocks.title: Mixing hot and cold water
blocks.q: $100\ \text{g}$ of water at $80^\circ\text{C}$ is mixed with $100\ \text{g}$ of water at $20^\circ\text{C}$ in an insulated cup. What is the final temperature?
steps: The hot water's energy loss equals the cold water's gain.
Same substance, same mass: each changes by the same number of degrees, so they meet halfway.

blocks.title: Bathtub or teacup?
blocks.q: Which has more thermal energy: a bathtub of water at $40^\circ\text{C}$ or a cup of tea at $80^\circ\text{C}$?
steps: The tea is at the higher temperature: its particles move faster on average.
The bathtub holds hundreds of times more water, so its total energy of motion is far larger.
blocks.a: The bathtub, though the tea is hotter.

blocks.html: Treating heat and temperature as the same thing, or thinking cold flows from a cold object into a warm one. Ice in your hand feels cold because heat leaves your hand and goes into the ice. Check any heat question by asking which object is hotter: energy always flows away from it.
Watch two objects reach the same temperature in Temperature and the Zeroth Law.

Heat and Temperature told you heat flows from hot to cold. How much the temperature changes depends on the material. A metal pan heats up in seconds; the water in it takes minutes. Rearranging one formula answers every question about it.

$$q = mc\Delta T$$ where $q$ is the heat (J), $m$ the mass (g), $\Delta T = T_{\text{final}} - T_{\text{initial}}$, and $c$ the specific heat: the energy needed to warm 1 g of the substance by $1^\circ\text{C}$, in J/(g·°C).

head: Substance
c, J/(g·°C)
blocks.cap: Specific heats (OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Table 5.1).

blocks.html: Heat goes into the motion of particles. A gram of lead holds far fewer atoms than a gram of aluminum, because lead atoms are almost 8 times heavier. Metals need about the same energy per mole of atoms to warm by a degree (multiply each $c$ above by its molar mass and you get about $25\ \text{J}$), so per gram, heavy-atom metals have low specific heats. Water's is high because its molecules also store energy by spinning and tugging on their hydrogen bonds.

blocks.name: ch-calorimeter
blocks.cap: Equal masses of copper (hot) and aluminum (cool). The same amount of heat leaves the copper and enters the aluminum, but the copper's temperature changes more, because its specific heat is lower.

blocks.title: Warming water
blocks.q: How much heat warms $50.0\ \text{g}$ of water from $20.0^\circ\text{C}$ to $45.0^\circ\text{C}$?

blocks.title: Finding a temperature change
blocks.q: $1{,}000\ \text{J}$ of heat flows into a $100.\ \text{g}$ block of iron. How much does its temperature rise?
steps: $\Delta T = 22.3^\circ\text{C}$. The same heat would warm $100\ \text{g}$ of water by only $2.39^\circ\text{C}$.

blocks.title: Identifying a metal
blocks.q: A $25.0\ \text{g}$ metal block absorbs $449\ \text{J}$ and warms by $40.0^\circ\text{C}$. Which metal in the table could it be?

blocks.html: Thinking a substance with a high specific heat warms up faster. It is the opposite: a high $c$ means many joules per gram per degree, so the temperature changes slowly. That is why water heats and cools slowly and helps keep coastal climates mild. Check: with the same $q$ and $m$, a bigger $c$ must give a smaller $\Delta T$.
Try materials with different specific heats in Temperature and the Zeroth Law.

Put a hot object into cool water inside an insulated cup and wait. Energy is conserved, so what one loses, the other gains. With q = mcΔT for each and an equation with the unknown on both sides, you can find a specific heat or a final temperature.

In an insulated calorimeter no heat escapes, so $$q_{\text{lost}} + q_{\text{gained}} = 0, \quad\text{or}\quad -q_{\text{hot}} = q_{\text{cold}}$$ The hot object's $q$ is negative (it loses heat) and the cold object's $q$ is positive.

Energy cannot be created or destroyed. If the cup lets no heat in or out, every joule that leaves the hot metal must end up in the water. Each object follows its own $q = mc\Delta T$, with its own mass, specific heat and temperature change, and both end at the same final temperature.

blocks.name: ch-calorimeter
blocks.cap: A hot iron block in a cup of water. The bars show the heat lost by the iron and gained by the water: always equal in size and opposite in sign.

blocks.title: Finding a specific heat
blocks.q: A $50.0\ \text{g}$ metal block at $95.0^\circ\text{C}$ is dropped into $100.0\ \text{g}$ of water at $22.0^\circ\text{C}$. Both end at $25.7^\circ\text{C}$. What is the metal's specific heat?

blocks.title: Finding the final temperature
blocks.q: A $100.0\ \text{g}$ copper block ($c = 0.385$) at $90.0^\circ\text{C}$ goes into $200.0\ \text{g}$ of water at $20.0^\circ\text{C}$. What is the final temperature?
blocks.a: $23.1^\circ\text{C}$: the water's large heat capacity keeps it near where it started.

blocks.html: Dropping the minus sign in $q_{\text{lost}} = -q_{\text{gained}}$, which leads to a negative specific heat or an impossible final temperature, or pairing the metal's mass with water's specific heat. Check: the final temperature must lie between the two starting temperatures, and every $q = mc\Delta T$ must use one object's own $m$, $c$ and $\Delta T$.
Explore heat flowing to equilibrium in Temperature and the Zeroth Law.

Heat a pot of ice steadily and watch a thermometer. The temperature rises, stops at $0^\circ\text{C}$ for a long while, rises again, then stops at $100^\circ\text{C}$. Heat and Temperature and the forces of Predicting Boiling Points explain the pauses.

During a phase change, such as melting or boiling, the temperature stays constant even though heat keeps flowing in. The added energy pulls particles apart from their neighbors instead of speeding them up. For water: $q = n\,\Delta H_{\text{fus}}$ to melt ($6.01\ \text{kJ/mol}$) and $q = n\,\Delta H_{\text{vap}}$ to boil ($40.7\ \text{kJ/mol}$).

On a sloped part of the curve, heat speeds the particles up, so their average kinetic energy (the temperature) rises. On a flat part, heat works against the attractions between molecules: it loosens them in melting and breaks them apart completely in boiling. Breaking molecules completely free takes far more energy than loosening them, which is why the boiling plateau is about 7 times longer. The bonds inside each water molecule are not broken: steam is still $\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$.

blocks.name: ch-heatingcurve
blocks.cap: A heating curve for $100\ \text{g}$ of water. Move the marker: on the flat parts the particle picture changes state while the temperature holds still.

blocks.title: Melting ice
blocks.q: How much heat melts $36.0\ \text{g}$ of ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$? ($\mathrm{H}_{2}\mathrm{O}$: $18.02\ \text{g/mol}$)
steps: The temperature does not change, so use the heat of fusion, not $mc\Delta T$.

blocks.title: Boiling water away
blocks.q: How much heat boils away $50.0\ \text{g}$ of water at $100^\circ\text{C}$?
steps: $q = 2.775 \times 40.7 = 113\ \text{kJ}$, nearly ten times the heat that melted $36\ \text{g}$ of ice.

blocks.html: Thinking the temperature keeps rising while ice melts, or that boiling water gets hotter the longer it boils. While both phases are present, the energy goes into changing the state, so the temperature stays at the melting or boiling point until the change is complete. Check on the graph: flat means a phase change.
Running the curve backward, a cooling curve has the same plateaus: freezing water and condensing steam release exactly the energy that melting and boiling took in.

A burning match gives off heat; an instant cold pack soaks it up. In Physical and Chemical Changes you saw that reactions make new substances; here you track the energy, the stored energy of Forms of Energy, as heat flows in or out.

Split the world into the system (the reacting substances) and the surroundings (everything else). An exothermic process releases energy to the surroundings, which warm up: $\Delta H < 0$. An endothermic process takes energy from the surroundings, which cool down: $\Delta H > 0$.

Chemical energy is stored in the arrangement of atoms and the bonds between them. If the products hold less chemical energy than the reactants, the difference leaves as heat (or light). If they hold more, the reaction must take that energy in. $\Delta H$ is the energy of the products minus that of the reactants, so its sign tells the direction of the flow.

blocks.cap: An energy diagram. The products sit below the reactants, so energy is released to the surroundings: an exothermic reaction with $\Delta H = -90\ \text{kJ}$. The hump is the activation energy you will meet later.

blocks.title: A cold pack
blocks.q: Squeezing an instant cold pack dissolves ammonium nitrate in water, and the pack gets cold. Is the process exothermic or endothermic?
steps: The system is the dissolving salt; the surroundings include the water, the bag and your hand.
The surroundings get colder, so they lost energy to the system.

blocks.title: Reading a diagram
blocks.q: On an energy diagram, the reactants are at $250\ \text{kJ}$ and the products at $100\ \text{kJ}$. Find $\Delta H$.

blocks.html: Mixing up the system and the surroundings. A cold pack feels cold because the reaction takes heat from your hand, not because it gives off "cold". Check: decide what is the system, then ask whether the surroundings warmed (exothermic) or cooled (endothermic).

Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions said the energy change of a reaction comes from rearranging atoms. With the bonds you drew in Lewis Structures, you can estimate that change by counting bonds broken and bonds formed.

Breaking a bond takes energy; forming a bond releases energy. $$\Delta H \approx \sum(\text{energies of bonds broken}) - \sum(\text{energies of bonds formed})$$ If forming the products' bonds releases more than breaking the reactants' bonds costs, the reaction is exothermic.

A bond is an attraction between atoms, so the bonded atoms sit in an energy "well". Pulling them apart means climbing out of the well, which always costs energy, just as pulling two magnets apart takes work. When new bonds form, atoms fall into new wells and the energy comes out. The bond energy is the depth of the well, the energy needed to break one mole of that bond.

blocks.html: Thinking that breaking a bond releases energy. It is a widespread idea, and it has the energy flowing the wrong way. When a fuel burns, the energy comes out as the new bonds in carbon dioxide and water form; breaking the old bonds costs energy. Check the signs: "broken" is energy in, "formed" is energy out.

blocks.html: Some reactions are over in a flash; others, like iron rusting, take years. Kinetic Molecular Theory pictures particles flying and colliding, and Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions showed that atoms must rearrange for a reaction to happen. Put these together and you can explain reaction speed.

For particles to react, they must collide, hard enough to reach the activation energy $E_a$, and lined up with the right orientation. Anything that makes such collisions more frequent speeds the reaction up: a higher temperature, a higher concentration (or gas pressure), or a larger surface area of a solid.

Most collisions are too gentle: the particles bounce apart unchanged. Raising the temperature does two things. Collisions happen a little more often, but, more importantly, many more of them carry at least $E_a$. For a reaction with $E_a = 50\ \text{kJ/mol}$, warming from $300\ \text{K}$ to $310\ \text{K}$ raises the collision rate by less than 2%, yet nearly doubles the share of collisions that are hard enough. Concentration and surface area act differently: they only add collisions, because more reactant particles are in reach of each other.

blocks.html: Thinking every collision makes a reaction, or that heating speeds a reaction only by causing more collisions. If every collision reacted, gases would react almost instantly. Most collisions bounce; heating mainly raises the fraction of collisions that have enough energy. Check any "why" answer about temperature: does it mention energy, not only frequency?

blocks.html: Collision Theory and Reaction Rate said that a collision must reach the activation energy to react. On an energy diagram, that requirement is a hill between the reactants and the products, and a catalyst is a way around it.

The activation energy $E_a$ is the climb from the reactants to the top of the energy hill. A catalyst provides a different pathway with a lower hill, so more collisions succeed and the reaction speeds up. The catalyst is not used up, and it does not change $\Delta H$: the reactants and products sit at the same energies as before.

A catalyst takes part in the reaction and is given back at the end. A metal surface, for example, holds reactant molecules so that their old bonds weaken as new ones start to form, and an enzyme's active site does the same for the molecules in a cell. The route changes; the starting point and the end point do not. A lower hill also helps the reverse reaction, so a catalyst speeds up both directions equally.

A catalyst comes out unchanged, which is why a car's catalytic converter keeps working for years and a little enzyme handles a lot of reaction. Check on the diagram: only the height of the hill changes.

Many reactions can run backward too. In a sealed flask, the products of colliding reactants collide with each other and re-form the reactants. What happens when both directions run at once?

A reversible reaction reaches equilibrium when the forward and reverse reactions run at equal rates. From then on the amounts of reactants and products stay constant, though both reactions keep going. Constant does not mean equal: the amounts can be very different.

At the start only reactants are present, so the forward reaction is fast and the reverse reaction cannot run. As reactants are used up, the forward rate falls; as products build up, the reverse rate rises. The two rates meet, and after that each molecule of product that forms is matched by one that turns back. It is like a crowded shop where people enter and leave at the same rate: the number inside holds steady while the people keep changing.

blocks.html: Thinking the reactions stop at equilibrium, or that the reactants and products must be present in equal amounts. Both reactions continue; only the rates are equal. Check: "equilibrium" is about rates being equal, not amounts.

A system at Dynamic Equilibrium holds steady until something disturbs it. Then it shifts to a new balance. Predicting the direction uses the rates you know, plus Boyle's Law for what squeezing a gas does.

Le Chatelier's principle: if a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a change in concentration, pressure (by changing the volume) or temperature, it shifts in the direction that partly undoes the change. A catalyst causes no shift.

blocks.html: Adding a reactant makes forward collisions more frequent, so the forward rate jumps ahead until the extra reactant is partly used and the rates match again. Squeezing a gas mixture raises the pressure; the side with fewer gas molecules makes fewer collisions with the walls, so shifting toward it lowers the pressure. For temperature, treat heat as a product of an exothermic reaction: adding heat pushes the reaction back. (Temperature is the one change that also changes the equilibrium constant, as you will see later.)

blocks.a: Toward the reactants: less ammonia at equilibrium.

blocks.html: Thinking a catalyst shifts an equilibrium, or that the shift undoes a change completely. A catalyst only gets the system to equilibrium sooner. And after nitrogen is added, the new equilibrium still has more nitrogen than before; the shift only takes back part of the change.

The ammonia industry balances these effects. High pressure (roughly 150 to 300 atm) favors ammonia; low temperature favors it too but makes the reaction too slow, so plants run at about 400 to 500 °C with an iron catalyst.

blocks.html: Every reaction so far moved electrons and left the nucleus alone. Some nuclei, though, are unstable: certain Isotopes and Mass Number have too many neutrons, too few, or are simply too big. They change on their own by giving off particles or energy, and when the number of protons changes, the atom becomes a different element.

In alpha decay a nucleus gives off a helium-4 nucleus (mass number $-4$, atomic number $-2$). In beta decay a neutron turns into a proton and an electron flies out (atomic number $+1$, mass number unchanged). In positron emission a proton becomes a neutron (atomic number $-1$). A gamma ray is pure energy: it changes neither number. In a nuclear equation the mass numbers balance and the atomic numbers balance.

blocks.html: The top number (mass number) counts protons plus neutrons, and nucleons are neither made nor destroyed, so the top numbers must add up the same on both sides. The bottom number counts charge (protons, or $-1$ for an electron), and charge is conserved too, so the bottom numbers must balance as well. Whatever atomic number the new nucleus has decides which element it is.

blocks.html: Radioactive Decay and Nuclear Equations described what happens to one nucleus. In a sample of billions, the decays follow a steady pattern, the halving kind of change from Exponential Functions.

The half-life is the time it takes for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay. After each half-life, half of what is left remains: after $n$ half-lives, the fraction left is $\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{n}$.

A radioactive nucleus does not age. In any given hour, each one has the same small chance of decaying, whether it formed a minute ago or a million years ago. So in each half-life, half of the nuclei that remain decay, whatever their number. The amount drops by the same fraction, not the same amount, in every equal stretch of time, which is exponential decay.

blocks.html: Radioactive Decay and Nuclear Equations changes a nucleus a little at a time. Two other nuclear changes are far more dramatic: splitting a heavy nucleus in two, or joining two light ones into one. Both release enormous amounts of energy.

Fission splits a heavy nucleus, such as uranium-235 after it absorbs a neutron, into two middle-sized nuclei and a few neutrons. Fusion joins light nuclei, such as isotopes of hydrogen, into a heavier one, such as helium. In both, the products have slightly less mass than the reactants, and that missing mass becomes energy: $E = mc^2$.

How tightly a nucleus holds together, per proton or neutron, depends on its size: the binding is strongest for nuclei near iron and nickel. Splitting a very heavy nucleus or joining very light ones both make nuclei that are more tightly bound, and the extra binding comes out as energy. Because $c^2$ is huge ($9.00 \times 10^{16}\ \text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$), a tiny loss of mass gives a vast amount of energy, millions of times more per gram than any chemical reaction.
